articles.title: Zadie Smith tells Dua Lipa inequality has made culture clashes feel ‘existential’
articles.summary:
Novelist says demise of Britain’s ‘incredible’ welfare system and housing struggles have led to deeper divisions

The novelist Zadie Smith has said that inequality has made culture clashes…

blocks.text: The novelist Zadie Smith has said that inequality has made culture clashes feel “existential”, adding that it has become “natural to look to your left and think ‘who the fuck are you?’”

In an interview with Dua Lipa as part of the Southbank Centre’s London literature festival, Smith argued that the demise of Britain’s “incredible, historic” welfare system has led to greater divisions.
The pair discussed Smith’s debut novel, White Teeth, which was published in 2000 and primarily set in the last three decades of the 20th century.

Asked by Lipa about how attitudes towards multiculturalism have changed since the 80s and 90s, and the current “dividing line” on immigration in UK politics, Smith pointed to increased inequality and unemployment.

“When you’re living in basically decent housing, when you hurt yourself you know you can go to hospital and be treated just like the rich kid down the road – then the differences [with others] become interesting, sometimes annoying, but not existential,” said the novelist.
“Now, they’re existential. When you can’t get a job, when there’s no housing, when your schools are falling apart, when the hospitals are falling apart – now it feels existential.”

White Teeth traces the stories of three families – the Joneses, the Iqbals and the Chalfens – and is set in Kilburn and Willesden in north-west London, where Smith grew up. The writer praised her state education, saying it has stood her “in incredibly good stead” throughout her life. “I can talk to anyone. The posh kids up the hill? Not so much.

“Now, when you look at my neighbourhood, the same schools, the same situations – everything is harder, everybody is poorer, everybody is struggling more,” she continued. “It becomes very, very natural to look to your left and think ‘who the fuck are you?’ That is an economic and structural question.”

Smith encouraged developing “a nostalgia for the left”. While “you don’t want the LGBTQ+ politics of the 80s, you don’t want the racial prejudice” depicted in White Teeth, “do you want the healthcare and the schools and the education? I think you do. So it’s about looking back and seeing what was of value – and what was [of] value to me was a social democracy that basically functioned, and might function again if people cared about it, wanted it, believed it could happen again.”

On the writing process for White Teeth – which she began when she was 21 and was published when she was 24 – Smith said that she finished the acclaimed novel in the aftermath of being broken up with and moving back in with her mum.

“Everybody else was out clubbing, I was like, ‘I’m fucking stuck in this room, finishing a novel,’” she said. But Valentine’s Day was approaching, and “all my girlfriends were like ‘we gotta go out, go on the pull’.” She ended up finishing it on 14 February and then “literally ran straight out to the club” – so the ending of the novel is “a chaos”, she said, adding that this is “why young people shouldn’t write novels”.
after newsletter promotion

Since White Teeth, Smith has written five novels – The Autograph Man, On Beauty, NW, Swing Time and The Fraud – along with short stories and nonfiction. Her most recent book was the essay collection Dead and Alive.

Lipa and Smith also discussed facing criticism for their works, with Lipa saying that “learning to live with reviews – bad reviews, good reviews” was “one of the hardest things for me to learn to deal with”. Smith said that literary criticism is “absolutely essential” because it “helps develop taste”.
“I’m very interested in criticism,” added Smith. “Even if it’s a bad review of me, if it’s well written, if it’s intelligent … I quite love ‘takedowns’.”

London literature festival runs until 1 November, with speakers selected by Lipa including Patti Smith, Malorie Blackman and Hisham Matar. Lipa runs a book club, Service95, through which she interviews authors on a monthly basis.

articles.title: Ageing users and record deaths – the data behind Britain’s £9.8bn-a-year cocaine habit
articles.summary: Sewage samples and crime statistics paint a picture of established users taking more cocaine, more often

blocks.text: From pub toilets and private parties to football terraces and far-right marches, cocaine has become a familiar presence across modern Britain. Deaths linked to the drug have risen to record levels, while its supply supports a multibillion-pound criminal industry.

But who is using the drug, and how has the picture changed? The figures do not necessarily show millions of new users, but highlight an established market in which some people take more cocaine, more often – and face greater harm as they grow older.
A £9.8bn-a-year habit?

In June this year the scientists at the Home Office published a new experimental estimate of cocaine consumption. Samples taken from sewage suggested that cocaine use rose by 26% between 2021 and 2025. They estimated that people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25: the equivalent of roughly 2.5bn lines, with an estimated street value of £9.8bn.

Yet crime survey data suggests the number of people reporting cocaine use in the past year has remained flat or fallen slightly since the pandemic. One explanation is that a similar or smaller number of people are using the drug more frequently. Another is that the survey excludes people who are homeless or living in institutions, and some respondents may be reluctant to admit to illegal drug use.

Dr Josh Torrance, a specialist in drug markets, says wastewater analysis can reveal use that surveys miss. Having surveyed festivalgoers, he said: “People are often not honest about their drug use with strangers.” Although sewage estimates have substantial margins of error, and the estimated street value should be taken with a pinch of salt, the direction of travel is broadly accurate.
Cheaper cocaine, until recently

For several years, the market offered cocaine at falling prices. The National Crime Agency (NCA) told the Guardian that wholesale prices dropped below pre-pandemic levels in 2022 and reached “historically low levels” in 2025. However, it has seen signs that wholesale prices are rising again in 2026.

Torrance tracks advertised prices for an ounce of cocaine from a pool of vendors. He says the price fell from about £1,300 in March 2022 to about £1,000 by August 2023. When he resumed collecting data in September 2025, it was about £700. That remained steady until June this year, when it rose to roughly £800; in July it reached £1,000. By September it had eased to about £950.

“I’ve never seen such a quick increase in the price of cocaine,” he says of the summer rise. He suspects a supply disruption, but says the cause is difficult to pin down in a market with many suppliers and routes.

High purity means that cheaper supply is more dangerous. Torrance says cocaine sold as “pure” is often about 70-80% pure, and a more diluted tier (sometimes marketed as “social cocaine”) may be about 60%. The NCA says wholesale purity has remained high in recent years. In Torrance’s view, “a reduced price drives up use. With increased use and increased purity, you end up with more deaths.”
White lines, grey hairs
Crime survey data – while subject to caveats – shows younger people are still the most likely to use the drug, but that use is falling among the young, and rising among older age groups.
Other statistics back this up. In England, 33,612 people started treatment for cocaine problems in 2024-25 – up 57% from 2019-20 – which also suggests an increase in frequent users.

Millennials seem to be the generation with the most problematic use. People in their 30s were the largest age group seeking help. Ten years earlier, it was those in their 20s. “We’ve seen a cohort of cocaine users age and continue to use cocaine,” says Torrance.
Fuel for violent crime
There has been a 10% rise in recorded crime rates mentioning cocaine since 2019, according to figures collected by the Guardian from 39 police forces.

Police recorded almost 30,000 crimes mentioning the word cocaine in 2025. Most were drug offences, but 18% were violent crimes, including stalking and harassment and one murder case. About 4% were sexual offences, including 344 rapes.
A police record mentioning cocaine does not by itself demonstrate cocaine use but the figures do give an indication of the direction of travel.

Home Office figures suggest that nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year. Those tested may be more likely to have used drugs than other domestic abuse suspects, but the figures highlight cocaine’s exacerbating role.
A deadly toll

More older people taking cocaine, increased purity on the streets, and a possible increase in frequent users have coincided with mounting harms, and not just for the victims of crime. A record number of people are now dying from taking cocaine in England and Wales. This rise has mainly been driven by older people, with more than half of cocaine deaths registered last year involving someone over 40.

Torrance says the ageing of a group that continues to use cocaine is reflected in hospital presentations and deaths. Acute overdose deaths often involve cardiac problems, he says, while the health effects of long-term use add to the risks.
An independent report last year found that the UK lacked a coordinated drug prevention strategy with dedicated funding, despite international evidence showing drug prevention programmes work.

“One reason cocaine deaths have risen so dramatically over the last five to 10 years is that we didn’t invest in upstream prevention,” Torrance says. Earlier drug education and helping people at risk engage with services would help.
“The more we can do that, the fewer of these issues we’ll see decades down the line.”

articles.title: Cocaine-linked crimes on the rise in Britain as consumption surges
articles.summary: Exclusive: Wastewater analysis in England suggests people took roughly 2.5bn lines of drug in one year

blocks.text: British police are recording a growing number of crimes linked to cocaine, including assaults, domestic abuse and dangerous driving, as figures show consumption has surged across England.

A Guardian investigation has found police forces across Britain recorded a 10% rise in crime rates associated with the class A drug since 2019, while the Home Office estimates cocaine usage at sites across England has risen by 26% since 2021.

Cocaine is a powerful and addictive stimulant that causes euphoria, overconfidence, restlessness and paranoia. Experts have warned its use can cause already fraught situations to escalate, potentially leading to violent incidents.

The rise in consumption in recent years can be partly explained by historically low costs, while purity levels have remained high. Analysis of wastewater suggests people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25. That’s equivalent to roughly 2.5bn lines of cocaine, at an estimated street value of almost £10bn.

Police recorded at least 29,922 crimes mentioning the word cocaine in 2025 – equivalent to 63.4 for every 100,000 people. That was up from 57.7 cases for every 100,000 in 2019. Figures up to May this year suggest that number could increase again in 2026 to about 64 cases in every 100,000 people – a rise of more than 10% over seven years.

Martin Gallagher, an author and organised crime expert who served as a police officer in Scotland for 28 years, said cocaine use had become normalised: “It went from being the drug of the social elite to being something taken off the cistern of a toilet in a local pub.”

A majority of cocaine-associated crimes last year were drug offences – but 18% were violent crimes, including stalking and harassment and one murder case. Just under 4% of crime reports mentioning the word cocaine were sexual offences, including 344 rapes.

Separate figures highlight cocaine’s role in domestic abuse cases. Nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year.

The data, drawn from the Home Office’s drug test on arrest programme, is not representative, as some tests were only taken after police already suspected drug use. However, the results tally with a 2023 pilot study that found 59% of domestic abuse suspects tested positive for cocaine or opiates.

Harry Sumnall, a professor in substance use at Liverpool John Moores University, said: “Scientific reviews have found no strong evidence that cocaine directly induces violent behaviour, but domestic violence is often rooted in power, and both perpetrators and survivors describe cocaine intoxication escalating loss of control and jealousy, leading to violent incidents, and making existing abuse more frequent and more severe.”
He cautioned that a mention of cocaine in a crime record did not prove the drug had caused the offence.

blocks.caption: Cocaine went from being ‘the drug of the social elite to being something taken off the cistern of a toilet in a local pub’. Photograph: Andriy Popov/Alamy

blocks.text: Separate DVLA data obtained by road safety charity IAM RoadSmart found that drug-driving offences overtook drink-driving offences for the first time last year. There were 30,707 drug offences added to driving licences (up by 28% since 2022), and 29,769 drink-driving offences (down by 17%) in 2025.
after newsletter promotion

Government figures suggest that cocaine and cannabis are the most common illegal drugs involved in road fatalities. Figures obtained by the RAC suggest that drug-drivers are far more likely to reoffend than drink-drivers – meaning a smaller subset of repeat drug-drivers could be behind the rise.

Paul Court, a deputy chief constable who is deputy lead for drugs for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, warned that demand for illegal drugs sustained a “highly profitable criminal market built upon violence, exploitation and intimidation”, and that police enforcement alone was not enough to solve the problem.

An independent report last year by the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs found that the UK lacked a coordinated drug prevention strategy with dedicated funding – despite international evidence showing drug prevention programmes work.

Court added: “We have to reduce demand, prevent people being drawn into drug use in the first place, reduce harm and ensure those whose offending or vulnerability is linked to drug dependency have opportunities to access treatment and support.”

The Guardian contacted all 45 police forces in the UK under the Freedom of Information Act requesting figures for crimes mentioning the word cocaine. Of these, 39 responded with data. Not every force had records for each year or a breakdown of the types of crime associated with the drug. London’s Metropolitan police were not able to provide any data.

Data was taken from keyword searches of police summary notes, so do not necessarily mean that cocaine formed part of the offence. The figures may include some crimes tangential to the drug – for example, if a witness stated someone was known to use cocaine. Other crimes, where the drug was misspelled or mentioned in a different part of the notes, may be missing.

articles.title: What schools will do amid intense heat during El Niño
articles.summary: How prepared is the Department of Education for the potential effects of El Niño?

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The education sector will not be spared when El Niño worsens in the coming months. Across the country, temperatures are expected to be warmer than usual, which would pose another threat to students’ learning.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara previously said government protocols would ensure that El Niño’s effects are mitigated in public schools.
How exactly is the Department of Education (DepEd) preparing for the impact of the weather phenomenon? Pending formal guidelines, here’s what we know so far:

In an interview with Rappler on Friday, October 23, Education Undersecretary Malcolm Garma said the DepEd is concerned that lost school days may increase due to high heat index levels. The heat index, or the temperature that the human body perceives, is measured using the air temperature and the relative humidity in a place at a given time.
Garma noted that the DepEd’s existing class suspension guidelines, issued back in June, already spell out learning continuity plans for schools.

The DepEd said that under Level 1-Hayo, face-to-face classes continue during manageable conditions. Schools can set scheduled water breaks, shift outdoor activities to early morning or shaded areas, and allow students to wear comfortable clothing or Physical Education attire.
At Level 2-Hinay, schools may adopt modified class days with structured home-based or hybrid learning.

Level 3-Hinga may be implemented when temperatures can cause heat cramps or heat exhaustion or there is loss of water supply. Learning packets, short activities, and broadcast resources may be used to reduce academic demands.

Once the heat index reaches 42°C and above, academic activities are suspended at Level 4-Hinto, focusing on safety checks and psychosocial support referrals, according to the class suspension guidelines.
Garma said self-learning modules, activity sheets, and other materials needed for alternative learning will be prepositioned before the peak months of intense heat.

In case actual conditions turn out to be worse than projected, Garma said school heads can adjust class schedules or recommend granular suspensions of face-to-face classes. But he added that the situation must be properly assessed.

“Hindi naman ‘yung school head ay basta-basta na lang siyang magpapauwi o magsu-suspend. So kailangan mai-vet ito ng [schools] division office…or [they should] even coordinate with the local government unit. Para sa gano’n, talagang hindi naman maabuso din ‘yung pagsususpende ng klase,” the DepEd official said.

(The school head cannot just decide to send students home or suspend classes. This must be vetted by the schools division office or they should even coordinate with the local government unit. This is to prevent abuse of class suspensions.)

“While we are looking after…the welfare of our learners, we also have to ensure that learning continues. At alam naman natin na pinakamainam pa din na learning delivery natin ay kung school-based ito or face-to-face (And we know that the best learning delivery is school-based or face-to-face),” he added.
Garma said the DepEd has ordered schools to make hydration facilities and equipment, such as safe drinking stations and water dispensers, accessible to learners and personnel.
The DepEd also told schools to repair water leaks immediately and coordinate closely with local water concessionaires for rationing contingencies.

Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian earlier raised the possibility of deploying community water depots to public schools. These depots are rainwater catchment equipment with built-in filtration systems to provide potable water during shortages. Garma said the DepEd welcomes such proposals.

Regarding health, Garma said school clinics will be ready to address medical concerns like heat stroke or dehydration. Additional support from local government units (LGUs) and the Department of Health will also be tapped for emergency response.

With El Niño also threatening agriculture and food supply, schools division offices and schools were directed to develop contingency menus for the school-based feeding program, partner with LGUs and cooperatives for local food sourcing, and maintain buffer stocks of shelf-stable commodities.
Garma said public schools can use their funding for maintenance and other operating expenses to buy additional ventilators like electric fans.
But the DepEd’s long-term solution is structural intervention.

“For old classrooms, we cannot change their designs; we can only do mitigation. But for those classrooms under construction and for future ones, we’ll make sure that there will be structural intervention such as high ceilings, insulated ceilings, and wide airflow,” he said in Filipino.
Garma also said the DepEd is exploring the possibility of institutionalizing the use of solar power in schools to reduce electricity costs and possibly provide air-conditioning.

The DepEd said its upcoming formal guidelines for El Niño-related measures will mandate schools to conduct integrated school-level risk assessments covering water supply reliability, classroom thermal safety, electricity resilience, and fire hazard prevention.

The set of guidelines is also expected to prohibit schools from charging or requiring parents to buy cooling equipment, connectivity, or specialized attire as a condition for alternative learning modalities. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Win Gatchalian: Marcoleta, Estrada suspensions on hold pending motions
articles.summary: The suspension of Senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada will be held in abeyance pending the final resolution of their motions for reconsideration, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said…

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 2:56pm

The suspension of Senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada will be held in abeyance pending the final resolution of their motions for reconsideration, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.
Gatchalian made the statement after confirming that the Senate had received the suspension orders from the Sandiganbayan.

“Nakakuha rin ako ng sulat galing kay Sen. Jinggoy at Sen. Marcoleta na i-hold muna in abeyance ang suspension dahil ang balita namin... magpa-file sila ng motion for reconsideration,” Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB.

(We also received letters from Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta asking that their suspensions be held in abeyance because we received reports that they would file motions for reconsideration.)
“Kapag nag-file ng motion for reconsideration, hindi muna sinususpinde until maging final na ang kanilang motion for reconsideration,” he added.
(If a motion for reconsideration is filed, the suspension will be deferred until the motion is finally resolved.)

Earlier this month, the Sandiganbayan’s Fifth Division ordered Estrada placed under preventive suspension for 90 days in connection with the plunder and graft charges he faces over his alleged involvement in the flood control projects scandal.
It was the second 90-day preventive suspension imposed on Estrada after the anti-graft court’s Second Division issued a similar order in June in connection with separate graft charges.

Meanwhile, the Sandiganbayan’s Third Division ordered Marcoleta placed under preventive suspension also for 90 days in connection with a plunder charge over alleged undeclared campaign contributions worth P75 million.
Gatchalian said Marcoleta and Estrada, along with Senator Loren Legarda, were not receiving their salaries because of their absences from office.

Earlier, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said criminal charges against Legarda and Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste were expected to be filed soon over an alleged failure by Leviste’s solar company to deliver contracted power supply.
Remulla, however, declined to give a timeline for the filing of the cases.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Win Gatchalian, Ping Lacson to authorities: Conduct safe arrest of Bato dela Rosa
articles.summary: Authorities should conduct a safe arrest of Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, who is now considered "armed and dangerous" by law enforcement officials.

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 2:30pm
Authorities should conduct a safe arrest of Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, who is now considered "armed and dangerous" by law enforcement officials.
Senator Sherwin Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB that the safety of Dela Rosa and the authorities tasked with arresting him are equally important.
"Sa enforcement agencies, dapat maging ligtas 'yung pag-aresto kay Sen. Bato," Gatchalian said Sunday. "Hindi pwedeng maging bayolente o may karahasan na mangyari."
(Enforcement agencies must conduct a safe arrest of Sen. Bato. No violence or cruelty should occur.)
"Importante ligtas siya at ligtas din ang law enforcement agencies... Importante na magkaroon ng maayos na pag-aresto sa kanya," he added.
(It's important that he and our law enforcement agencies are safe. It is important to have an orderly arrest.)
'Due process'
In a statement on Sunday, Senator Panfilo Lacson shared the same sentiment, saying that Dela Rosa's arrest should be carried out peacefully and without tragedy.

"He (dela Rosa) has his faults, as we all do. But whatever accusations he faces, he is entitled to due process, a fundamental right guaranteed to every Filipino, and for that matter, to every human being," Lacson said
The Department of the Interior and Local Government has raised a P50-million reward for the arrest of dela Rosa, Secretary Juanito Victor "Jonvic" Remulla announced Friday.
Remulla's announcement came after he said Dela Rosa is under the protection of a group in Mindanao, with whom the government is initiating negotiations. He did not identify the said group.
He said an operation to get the former Philippine National Police chief could result in 10,000 deaths.
For Gatchalian, the government should assert its authority as he described the group to be more bolder than the former.
"Parang ang lumalabas, itong armed group ay mas matapang pa sa gobyerno," Gatchalian said.
(It seems like the armed group is more bold than the government.)
"Ang gobyerno, hindi dapat nakikipag-negotiate sa armed group lalo kung ang armed group ay terrorist group," he added.
(It's not right that the government is the one negotiating with the armed group, especially if that armed group is a terrorist group.)

Dela Rosa is charged before the International Criminal Court as a co-perpetrator with former president Rodrigo Duterte for cases of murder and attempted murder tied to the war on drugs of the latter's administration.
Both Duterte and Dela Rosa have denied the allegations against them.
Dela Rosa left the Senate before dawn on May 14, hours after a shooting incident in the chamber's premises.
Gatchalian said he has yet to communicate with Dela Rosa after his last appearance in May. —RF, GMA News

The Office of the Ombudsman files charges against former DPWH Region 12 regional director Subair Saro Diron, former assistant regional director Laureano Suan Jr., and several other DPWH personnel and private individuals

items: The Office of the Ombudsman has filed malversation and graft cases against two former DPWH officials, four personnel, and seven private individuals related to a road right-of-way scam in General Santos City.
Evidence was found against former DPWH officials and personnel for falsifying documents and inflating claims for land compensation, resulting in over P491 million in fraudulent payments.
The Ombudsman also ordered the dismissal of former DPWH Region 12 legal officer Ansare Mariga Busran in a separate administrative decision.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman has filed malversation and graft cases against two former Department of Public Works and Highways officials, four DPWH personnel, and seven private individuals over their alleged involvement in a road right-of-way scam in General Santos City.

The Office of the Ombudsman said in a press statement on Sunday, October 25, that it “found prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction” against former DPWH Region 12 regional director Subair Saro Diron, former assistant regional director Laureano B. Suan Jr., and DPWH personnel Tomas Marquez Rodriguez, David Lucena Padlan, Paisal Amerol Padate, and Ansare Mariga Busran.

The Ombudsman also included seven private individuals in the cases filed before the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan: Wilma Mamburam, Nelson Ti, Evelyn Paloso, Rudy Hadji Ong, Marisa Seguirre, William Uy, Paul Michael Bagio.

“The Ombudsman filed 18 informations for Malversation of Public Funds or Property through Falsification of Public Documents under Article 217 in relation to Article 171 of the Revised Penal Code, and another 18 informations for violation of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act,” the Office of the Ombudsman said.

In 2018 and 2019, the National Bureau of Investigation submitted three investigation reports to the Ombudsman in relation to the DPWH Region 12 payment for right-of-way for 18 parcels of land allegedly affected by the construction of the Digos-Makar National Road in Lagao, General Santos City.

The witness, Roberto Catapang Jr., had admitted in his 2017 affidavit that he was involved in a syndicate that was allegedly “in collusion with respondent public officers, collected money from the government purportedly as payments for the acquisitions, by fabricating and submitting fake documents.”

Investigators found that the claimants, which were paid a total of P491,931,120.20, had presented falsified documents. The DPWH Region XII technical working group had approved the disbursement of the amount to the claimants.

“Investigators also uncovered the alleged unlawful use of a 2009 appraisal value of P3,500 per square meter to determine compensation for properties taken by the government in the early 1990s, resulting in inflated right-of-way claims,” the Office of the Ombudsman said.
The press statement also said that in a separate administrative decision, the Ombudsman ordered the dismissal from service of former DPWH Region 12 legal officer Ansare Mariga Busran. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘That’s the way the city works’: how the UAE changed the face of Andy Burnham’s Manchester
articles.summary: The story of the emirates’ presence in Manchester winds from the Arab Spring to some of the most deprived places in England – with complicated results Emirati-linked firms’ ownership of Manchester…

blocks.text: When Hosni Mubarak, Egypt’s long-ruling dictator, was toppled from power in the Arab spring protests of 2011, his downfall sent shock waves across the Middle East. It also helped change the face of modern Manchester.
Mubarak’s successor, the Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohamed Morsi, was a sworn enemy of the United Arab Emirates, whose rulers feared the advance of Morsi’s Islamism.

The UAE, a key western ally, was concerned that David Cameron’s UK government was not strong enough on the Muslim Brotherhood and warned ministers it could pull billion-pound arms deals if Britain did not act.
A secret Whitehall unit was hastily established to keep the oil-rich emirates on side. Lucrative investment deals were offered in private meetings later revealed by the Guardian.
One of these would turn Abu Dhabi’s now crisis-stricken ownership of Manchester City football club into a much deeper stake in the city itself.

blocks.caption: An aerial view of the Etihad Stadium, the home of Manchester City, with the Ancoats and New Islington neighbourhoods in the background. Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: Fifteen years after the Egyptian revolution, a Guardian analysis can reveal a stark rise in the amount of land and property owned by the UAE government or Emirati developers in Manchester over the past decade – extending to the size of 260 football pitches at its peak in 2023.

Manchester City’s owner, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, has built an extensive portfolio outside the club, including the UK’s biggest indoor arena, an “upper-upscale hotel” that opened last month, a suite of apartment blocks and investment in world-leading university research through a firm run by Khaldoon al-Mubarak, the City chief executive.
The cheating scandal at Manchester City has put the spotlight on the wider influence of Abu Dhabi in the city, the growth of which helped power Andy Burnham to Downing Street.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham, then mayor of Manchester, speaking to Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium in September 2019. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

blocks.text: Through interviews with key past and present local politicians and officials, new data analysis and an examination of public records spanning more than a decade, the Guardian can now tell the story of how the oil-rich state’s influence has grown, what it has meant for Manchester, and how it has fuelled concerns about the city becoming “a northern version of London”.
‘We were seeking a very significant investment’

Ten years ago, the sight of the murky-green Rochdale canal was a sign you had strayed too far out of Manchester’s lively Northern Quarter and should turn back. Now drinkers and diners gravitate to the area, pulled in by trendy waterside bars serving up £6.90 pints and an artisanal bakery where a single croissant costs £7.50.

blocks.caption: New Islington marina, part of the new, modern Ancoats. Photograph: Mark Waugh/The Guardian

blocks.text: That transformation began in summer 2013, when David Cameron’s government sought to defuse tensions with the UAE and asked Manchester city council to draw up three investment proposals for the super-rich emirates.

One of these resulted in a £1bn deal called Manchester Life, under which the council sold a prime slice of city centre land to Abu Dhabi for £5m to build 6,000 homes, along with a right of first refusal on other projects.

Richard Leese, the leader of Manchester city council at the time, told the Guardian: “That was a UK government-brokered deal and we were obviously seeking a very significant investment for what would in total have been a £1bn scheme.

“Housing development in and around the city centre and Ancoats in particular had stopped and been stopped for several years. At that time there were no [other] developers who were either willing or able to do it.”

blocks.caption: Richard Leese wearing a City scarf in Manchester town hall in May 2010 when he was the leader of the city council. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: In a press release, Leese hailed the partnership as a “world-class exemplar of regeneration” and “a platform for the delivery of more than 6,000 new homes”.

However, only 2,039 homes have been delivered by Manchester Life – a third of the total promised – with a further 2,839 homes being built by other developers. The total of 4,878 new properties is nearly 20% short of the 6,000 envisaged.

Despite the council’s longstanding policy of at least 20% of new developments being for social and affordable housing, only 8% of these 4,878 properties fell into that category – and none were provided by Manchester Life.

blocks.caption: Homes-to-rent adverts in New Islington. Photograph: Mark Waugh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Food banks and luxury flats

A five-minute walk from the new Abu Dhabi-funded apartments, which are home to the city’s first Michelin-starred restaurant, the nave of a former Methodist church is stacked high with emergency food for those living on surrounding streets.

The short walk to the Etihad Stadium includes some of the poorest areas in the second most deprived local authority in England. Within only half a mile, there are four charity food banks or distribution sites, one of which has a plaque marking its opening by Burnham in 2021.

“It’s bound to cause resentment,” said Mark Blake, the chief executive of Manchester Central Foodbank, of the sudden influx of shiny apartments, expensive eateries and well-paid tenants. “When it’s in your face and is during a cost of living crisis it potentially could lead to some unrest. I think it should be a real concern.”

blocks.caption: The food bank at Trinity Ancoats. Photograph: Mark Waugh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Parking has become a flashpoint, with reports of cars being vandalised after being left on council estate streets by those living or dining at the Abu Dhabi-funded properties. Tenants of the swanky apartments are encouraged to leave food to local food banks in donation boxes in each of the luxury blocks.

“People are feeling all these cultural divides that are played out through the proxy of housing and everyday issues around parking,” said Alan Good, a Lib Dem councillor for Ancoats and Beswick. “Residents tell me they look at the shiny new towers and there’s a resentment – a feeling that they’re not benefiting from what Manchester is benefiting from.”
Good said he felt Manchester was becoming a “northern version of London” as an “insane” property crisis compounded the misery for the city’s 20,000 people on the social housing register.

Dr Matthew Stallard, a University College London researcher and chair of trustees at Manchester Central Foodbank, said there was an uncomfortable disconnect between the city’s reputation nationally – with “Manchesterism” becoming a byword for a thriving metropolis with an eye on broader social benefits – and the reality for many in the city.

blocks.caption: Matthew Stallard, the chair of trustees at Manchester Central Foodbank, in Ancoats. Photograph: Mark Waugh/The Guardian

blocks.text: “If you look at central Manchester and all the skyscrapers and you go out in every direction by a mile and a half or two miles, you’re then in some of the most deprived neighbourhoods in the country. In Ancoats, it’s a very clear line where the money is and where the money’s not.”
Awkward questions

In summer 2016, Burnham was keenly aware of Greater Manchester’s housing crisis. He told the Salford Star that if elected, he would stop large property firms benefiting from multimillion-pound taxpayer-funded loans from the mayoral authority.

There were concerns, he said, that the Greater Manchester combined authority (GMCA) fund had “been used to provide loans to large companies, which should have used their own finance instead, and that is too focused on city centre and luxury schemes”.

Barely a year later, Burnham signed off a £55m loan to Jersey-registered property firms owned by Sheikh Mansour, scion of one of the world’s wealthiest families with a reported fortune of about £300bn.

blocks.caption: Sheikh Mansour speaks with the Manchester City player Pablo Zabaleta and manager Pep Guardiola during a training camp in Abu Dhabi in 2017. Photograph: Victoria Haydn/Manchester City FC/Getty Images

blocks.text: GMCA said its loans fund was available to all developers who met the lending criteria and that the loans had been repaid in full. But these decisions are now being investigated by councillors on GMCA’s scrutiny committee.

There are awkward questions for Burnham, too. Weeks before the loans were approved, he enjoyed hospitality from City’s owners in a meeting that came to light only last week after disappearing from public records. The prime minister initially said he had had only one “significant” meeting with the club’s bosses – in 2021 – but a further five have since emerged.
Burnham said last week he had asked GMCA to conduct a “manual trawl of everything, as I want everything possible to be out there”. He added: “There’s no question about that – full transparency.”
There appeared to be little transparency, however, when it came to the council’s long-term relationship with Manchester City’s owners.

In December 2015, it signed a 10-year “collaboration agreement” with Abu Dhabi giving the emirates first refusal on land near the city centre. A specific clause in effect gagged the council’s democratically elected politicians from announcing the deal without written approval from Sheikh Mansour’s firm.

blocks.caption: Modern apartments in the New Islington area. Photograph: Mark Waugh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Other Manchester developers only discovered this years later. “It’s blatant partiality on a massive scale. It stinks,” said one property consultant. A council spokesperson defended the clause as “a standard agreement between two parties that ensures announcements or information releases are agreed by all parties”.

All of the property, now worth an estimated £350m, is ultimately owned by Sheikh Mansour via Jersey-domiciled subsidiaries, with the super-rich Emirati receiving the rent paid by the hundreds of mostly young professionals who live there.

The council said it had received nearly £3m as part of an undisclosed profit-sharing agreement and a further £17.6m in council tax. However, the precise return to the taxpayer – and the terms under which the deals were struck – remain unknown.

Leese, 75, stepped down as council leader after 25 years in December 2021, becoming honorary president at Manchester City two years later. When approached by the Guardian, he denied the Abu Dhabi deal was shielded from scrutiny and defended his appointment at Manchester City.
“This was something that happened after I retired from the council. Whether it would have been appropriate when I was on the council, I would have questioned that,” Leese said.

One senior former council officer, who worked in the property and development team, described the culture in this period as “Kremlin-like” or akin to “a medieval court” where officials could show “no dissent” towards the decisions of the Labour leadership.

“When you’ve got a council that’s 99% one party, there wasn’t really room for discussion,” they said, adding that they felt some senior leaders got “blinded by schmoozing around” with Abu Dhabi executives and others.

Leese denied he got too close to Manchester City, the team he supports, or gave them favourable treatment as council leader. “There are a lot of players in Manchester that the city council is close to,” he said.

blocks.caption: Manchester City players lifting the Premier League trophy in 2018. Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty

blocks.text: “That’s the way the city works – in partnership.”

Manchester city council has strongly denied claims of a “sweetheart deal” with Abu Dhabi after researchers at the University of Sheffield concluded it had “sold the family silver too cheaply” by giving the land to Abu Dhabi at a cheaper rate than comparable developments.
The future No 10 North

In 2017, three years after the first Abu Dhabi deal and the year Burnham became Greater Manchester mayor, council leaders made another huge bet. They paid £42m for a hollowed out retail park next to the £1bn Manchester Life development, described at the time as the biggest ever land purchase in Manchester city centre.
Its price was at least six times higher per acre than the adjacent land sold for £5m to Sheikh Mansour – and it would later be identified as the permanent future home of Burnham’s No 10 North.

This former retail park was also a partnership with Abu Dhabi. Again, the terms were shielded from scrutiny as members of the public were excluded from council hearings – but inside the town hall, the fallout was significant.

blocks.caption: The former central retail park being cleared. Photograph: Mark Waugh/The Guardian

blocks.text: A senior council property officer, Dominic Hayes, resigned abruptly in March 2018 over concerns about the deals the council was doing with Mansour’s group. He listed a series of complaints in an email to the council chief executive, Joanne Roney, who the previous year had succeeded the all-powerful Howard Bernstein when he retired after 29 years in charge.

In a tense meeting days after the resignation, a senior council figure, Eddie Smith, is said to have told colleagues that Hayes had thrown them “under a bus” and that the leadership was furious. According to contemporaneous notes by a colleague, seen by the Guardian, Smith said Hayes had made “not acceptable [and] possibly dangerous” criticisms of a Manchester City board member who was a key figure in the Manchester Life deal.

Smith is then said to have commented: “You don’t criticise the council’s relationship with the football club in this organisation and hope to survive.” Smith, who left the council in 2020, denies making the comment.

Yet Hayes’ concerns were serious enough to warrant an internal investigation into governance at the council. It found that anxieties about the council’s deal-making were not limited to just one officer.

A second senior employee told auditors they were concerned that the council had “overpaid” for the rundown retail park, according to an official record of the meeting. That officer raised concerns that the Abu Dhabi-led project was “driving the master planning for a site they didn’t own”.
When Burnham became prime minister in July, the site was tipped as the permanent home for No 10 North. As scrutiny of the Abu Dhabi link grew in October, these plans were quietly shelved.
‘The fragility of the Manchester model’
Council sources noticed a change of approach under Leese’s successor, Bev Craig, when she became council leader in December 2021.

blocks.caption: Bev Craig in 2021, the year she was appointed leader of Manchester city council. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: Craig ordered a review of the Manchester Life deal to make sure it was “all legal, all above board”, she told BBC Radio Manchester this month, adding: “The answer was yes.”

One of the reviews commissioned by Craig, who succeeded Burnham this year as Greater Manchester mayor, was published in July. It found that while the deals with developers such as Abu Dhabi had delivered “significant benefits”, there were “weaknesses in documentation, monitoring and assurance”, particularly around the profit-sharing nature of these deals.

Prof Jonathan Silver, a University of Sheffield researcher who has analysed the Manchester Life deal, said the growing buy-up of land and property by Emiratis raised “major concerns about the fragility of the ‘Manchester model’ and its reliance on attracting flows of international finance, whatever the cost”.

Silver said there were “urgent questions” about what would happen to the hundreds of homes in the Manchester Life developments if Sheikh Mansour was forced or decided to sell Manchester City in light of the cheating scandal.

Leese remains confident the Abu Dhabi deals were a huge success for the city. Asked whether he would have handled the partnership any differently given the concerns raised by academics and others, he said: “No. Nothing that I can think of. It is a phenomenally good deal for Manchester.”
Additional reporting: Carmen Aguilar García and Michael Goodier

articles.title: ‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder’: Palestinians fear the worst from Israel election
articles.summary: Humanitarian catastrophe largely ignored as rivals Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu vow to end Hamas rule As Israel prepares to go to the polls , Palestinians in Gaza are bracing for an outcome…
articles.byline: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Lorenzo Tondo

blocks.text: As Israel prepares to go to the polls, Palestinians in Gaza are bracing for an outcome that could shape their future, knowing their fate rests with the country that has reduced much of the territory to rubble and killed nearly 75,000 people.
Gaza, where nearly a million displaced Palestinians face dire sanitary conditions, water shortages and the constant threat of Israeli strikes, has been largely absent from the election campaign.

Both Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition and Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition Yashar party have focused instead on the goal of destroying Hamas in the wake of the 7 October attacks and the trauma inflicted on Israeli society. The humanitarian catastrophe unfolding just across the border has received little, if any, attention.

“We hope a government will come to power that is less inclined towards killing, displacement and our extermination,” said Sami Abu Rumi, 47, from Rafah, who is now displaced in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. “But, ultimately, we see the thinking of Israeli governments as largely similar.”

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot championed the “Dahiya doctrine” in the 2006 war with Hezbollah, which advocated overwhelming force against civilian areas where militants operated. Photograph: Ariel Schalit/AP

blocks.text: Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has set out a clear plan for Gaza’s future. Both have vowed to end Hamas rule and both support Donald Trump’s controversial peace plan.
Eisenkot, the former military chief whose party is leading Netanyahu’s Likud in the polls, has pledged to restore Israel’s international standing after three years of war. Yet he is no dove.

A senior commander during Israel’s 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot, whose son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza, later championed the “Dahiya doctrine”, which advocated overwhelming force against civilian areas where militants operated. Critics say the strategy has since been employed in Gaza, causing widespread destruction that, they argue, amounts to war crimes.

“Eisenkot talks of defeating Hamas, while Netanyahu boasts about military operations and the killing of Palestinians,” said Abu Rumi. ‘‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder. Meanwhile, families here struggle to feed their children, keep them in school and access medical care. With homes and infrastructure destroyed, simply surviving has become a daily struggle.”

Earlier this week, the Arab-led Joint List party in Israel aired a 48-second election video showing drone footage of Gaza’s ruins. “[We] behave as if everything that has happened here is completely normal,” the voiceover says. “As if tens of thousands of people weren’t killed here … as if entire cities were not destroyed and turned into wastelands.”
The party vows it “will not be silent”, adding: “[The other parties] want more destruction. We offer life.”

The chances of Arab parties joining an Eisenkot-led coalition are slim to none, although they could offer support from outside government. Yet among Palestinians in Gaza, pessimism runs deep: whoever wins, little is expected to change.

“I do not believe anyone genuinely cares about Gaza or has its people’s interests at heart,’’ said Haneen Hamdouna, 45, from Beit Lahia, who has also been displaced to al-Mawasi. ‘‘Whether it is Netanyahu, Eisenkot or someone else, attacking Gaza seems to have become part of Israeli election campaigning.

“For years, we have said that the incoming government might be better than the one before it, only to be shocked when it turns out to be worse. Perhaps 200 trucks would be allowed into Gaza instead of 100, but that would not mean any real change in our lives.”

In Gaza, most people are too preoccupied by the struggle to find food and water to follow the election campaign. Fears of renewed hunger are mounting as markets run short of fresh produce and other essentials.

Residents say commercial deliveries have been suspended for about a week, driving up prices. Flour now costs more than three times its previous price, while dwindling humanitarian aid has left families increasingly vulnerable to another food crisis.

blocks.caption: Candidates in the upcoming Israeli election include Yair Golan of the Democrats party (left billboard) and the Arab-led Joint List. Photograph: Amir Cohen/Reuters

blocks.text: Yet, some people in Gaza are following the Israeli elections closely, driven less by hope of change than fear of what the outcome could mean for their future.

They fear that Palestinian suffering has become a recurring feature of Israeli election campaigns, with candidates competing over who can take the toughest stance towards Gaza rather than offering any prospect of a better future.

“A friend was supposed to hold his son’s wedding in the coming days,” said Karim Mareesh, 43. “But he decided to postpone it until after the Israeli elections. He feared that the far-right government might secure another term, prompting the war to resume and forcing him to flee again. He could lose his tent and the wedding supplies he had struggled to save up for.”

Hope is hard to find in Gaza, where three years of war have reduced entire neighbourhoods to wastelands of shattered concrete and bomb craters. It is harder still to imagine a future when Israeli restrictions on food and humanitarian aid have turned hunger into a weapon of war. And almost impossible to see any light at the end of the tunnel when more than 20,000 Palestinian children have been killed since 7 October 2023.

“I feel that everything said about addressing our suffering is nothing more than an attempt to soothe our pain, or simply words and promises that we no longer believe,” says Noor AlMoghanni, 20, from Gaza City.
“Whether Netanyahu wins or loses, the reality here will not change. As I see it, their goal is to destroy Gaza and the foundations of life here.”

articles.title: Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?
articles.summary: Ukraine needs another satellite internet service, but a decent alternative to Elon Musk's network doesn't exist - yet.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
A man offers residents in Kherson, Ukraine, the use of his Starlink internet after a Russian strike
Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet.

Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network.
There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation.
France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared with Starlink's 10,000-plus.
The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, Iris², however it won't be up and running until 2029.
For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death.
"God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line."
For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones.
That vulnerability was highlighted by Musk himself on Saturday when he accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people".
Saying that loophole was closed last week, he wrote on X: "Violation of those terms will result in end of service."
He added: "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately".
Watch: Who controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?
Why does Starlink dominate in Ukraine?
Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years.

Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks.
"You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations.
Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored, highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate.
"Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted.
Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Musk.

While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS.
"This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ukrainian soldiers set up a Starlink terminal on the battlefield

blocks.text: Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/ Getty Images
Ukrainian soldiers set up a Starlink terminal on the battlefield
Starlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to agree.

Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield", a soldier said.
The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone.

Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones", said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company.
They are also about five times more expensive, she added.
What can the EU offer right now?
Rhetoric from the White House - like Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC.

She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon.

Comments from Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted, external at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable.
Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently", a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC.

Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom.
But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for.

That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs.

blocks.caption: Image caption, French President Emmanuel Macron, with a Eutelsat terminal, at the International Paris Air Show last year

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
French President Emmanuel Macron, with a Eutelsat terminal, at the International Paris Air Show last year

Eva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing because, as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive.

Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve".
No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield.
But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage."
Iris² - The EU's future network
Govsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, Iris², external is up and running in 2029.

The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one.
Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE.
It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen.

"Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that Iris² is planning for less satellites."
Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid".

blocks.caption: Image caption, A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, carrying 56 Starlink satellites, takes off from Cape Canaveral in March

blocks.text: Image source, Paul Hennessy/ Getty Images
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, carrying 56 Starlink satellites, takes off from Cape Canaveral in March
A highly produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With Iris², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity."
So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea.
"Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity."

It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare."
But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war."
Iris² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE, external announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences.
And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases.
Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need "a lot of money".
Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years.
"Even if you gave me €8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained.
Why Space is the new defence frontier
Military work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare.

"Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now."

While we look to the skies, however, most of the world's communications are travelling via undersea cables - about 99% in fact. But these are vulnerable to attack - this week the UK government outlined new measures to protect its cables, after an increase in suspicious activity by Russian vessels.
"In a crisis or conflict, there are serious concerns that undersea cables will be cut... so if that happens it's good to have satellite communication as a backup," Kari Bingen said.
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko

articles.title: Ombudsman charges 7 DPWH personnel over P491.9-M right-of-way 'scam'
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has filed 36 criminal counts against seven current and former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) personnel over alleged irregularities in P491.9 million in…

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 1:38pm

The Office of the Ombudsman has filed 36 criminal counts against seven current and former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) personnel over alleged irregularities in P491.9 million in right-of-way payments for a road project in General Santos City.

In a statement, the Ombudsman said the cases filed before the Sandiganbayan involve malversation of public funds through falsification of public documents and violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.
Those charged include former DPWH Region 12 (Soccsksargen) regional director Subair Saro Diron and former assistant regional director Laureano B. Suan Jr., along with five other agency personnel.

The charges comprise 18 counts of malversation of public funds through falsification of public documents under Articles 217 and 171 of the Revised Penal Code, and 18 counts of violating Republic Act 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.
Six private individuals were also named in the cases for their alleged participation in the scheme.
The charges arose from payments made for 18 parcels of land supposedly affected by the construction of the Digos-Makar National Road in Barangay Lagao, General Santos City.
The National Bureau of Investigation submitted three reports on the alleged irregularities in 2018 and 2019, prompting the Ombudsman's investigation.

In an affidavit executed in 2017, witness Roberto Catapang Jr. acknowledged his involvement in a group that allegedly worked with government officials to obtain public funds by submitting fabricated documents for purported land acquisitions.
The DPWH Soccsksargen technical working group subsequently approved P491,931,120.20 in payments to claimants whose supporting documents were later found to be falsified, the Ombudsman said.

Investigators also questioned the use of a 2009 property appraisal rate of P3,500 per square meter to compute compensation for land acquired by the government in the early 1990s. The valuation allegedly led to inflated claims for right-of-way payments.
In a separate administrative ruling, the Ombudsman ordered the dismissal of former DPWH Region 12 legal officer Ansare Mariga Busran from government service.—MCG, GMA News

articles.title: China rocket debris may have fallen in PH waters --PhilSA
articles.summary: The Philippine Space Agency on Sunday said China launched its Long March 8A rocket and its debris may have fallen in Philippine waters.

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 1:37pm
The Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA) on Sunday said China launched its Long March 8A rocket and its debris may have fallen in Philippine waters.
"The Long March 8A rocket was launched from the Hainan International Commercial Launch Center in Wenchang, Hainan, at around 10:03AM PhST on 25 October 2026," PhilSA said.
The agency said the debris from the rocket launch may have fallen within the following drop zones:

items: Drop Zone 1: approximately 107 NM (nautical miles) away from Patag Island, 122 NM away from Bajo de Masinloc, 164 NM away from El Nido, Palawan, and 167 NM away from Busuanga, Palawan; and
Drop Zone 2: 42 NM away from Hadji Muhtamad, Basilan, 42 NM away from Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park, 53 NM away from Pangutaran Island, Sulu, and 122 NM away from Puerto Princesa, Palawan.

blocks.text: PhilSA said Drop Zone 1 is within the Philippine Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), while Drop Zone 2 is within Philippine archipelagic waters.
A Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) was issued to warn pilots of an "aerospace flight activity," it added.
PhilSA also said unburned debris from rockets are expected to be discarded as the rocket enters outer space.

"While not projected to fall on land features or inhabited areas, falling debris poses danger and potential risk to ships, aircraft, fishing boats, and other vessels that will pass through the drop zone," it said.
The debris may also float around the area and wash toward nearby coasts, PhilSA said.
"Additionally, the possibility of an uncontrolled re-entry to the atmosphere of the rocket’s upper stages returning from outer space cannot be ruled out at this time," it said.
PhilSA advised the public to inform local authorities if they see any suspected debris.
It also advised against retrieving or coming in close contact with the suspected debris as these may contain toxic substances such as rocket fuel. —KG, GMA News
