articles.title: Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes
articles.summary:
PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint

Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of…

blocks.text: Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families, in collective punishment for a militant attack on an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.

The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.

Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.

blocks.caption: Israeli forces demolish a Palestinian house in Hebron on Friday. Photograph: Mussa Qawasma/Reuters

blocks.text: People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.

The large-scale demolitions follow an attack on Friday on an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20 minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.

The attack came four days before Israeli elections, and the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.

Netanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.
Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.

A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.

A Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”
Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.

“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”
The Israeli army was approached for comment on the operations and on videos showing extensive devastation.

articles.title: FFCCCII warns against declaring Chinese envoy Jing Quan persona non grata
articles.summary: The Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Inc. (FFCCCII) on Saturday cautioned against declaring Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata, warning that the move…

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 8:34pm

The Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Inc. (FFCCCII) on Saturday cautioned against declaring Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata, warning that the move could prompt reciprocal action against the Philippine ambassador to Beijing.

In a social media update by GMA News reporter Vonne Aquino, FFCCCII president Victor Lim urged the Chinese Embassy and the Philippine government to engage in dialogue and ease tensions instead of trading accusations online.
Lim also warned that the dispute could affect trade relations between the Philippines and China.
“Sana ’wag… calm down na lang para our economy will be moving forward,” Lim said.
(I hope they don’t. They should just calm down so our economy can continue moving forward.)
On Tuesday, a Senate resolution was filed urging President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. to declare Jing persona non grata or ask the Chinese government to recall him.
Calls for the ambassador’s expulsion intensified after he said Beijing could “easily win” if it resorted to force against the Philippines.
In response to the Senate resolution, the Chinese Embassy in Manila warned of reciprocal action if its diplomats were declared unwelcome.
“Since you don’t welcome us, we don’t welcome you, either. Fair enough,” the embassy said in a Facebook post.
Malacañang has deferred to the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on the matter, noting that Marcos does not favor declaring foreign envoys persona non grata.

“Hindi rin nais ng Pangulo itong mga pangyayaring palitan ng mga maaanghang na salita. Nais ng Pangulo, again, maganda na relasyon,” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said earlier this week.
(The President also does not want these exchanges of harsh words. The President wants good relations.)
The Palace also maintained that the President and his administration consider relations between the Philippines and China to be good.
The DFA summoned Jing on Monday to convey the Philippines’ “serious concern and strong objection” to his remarks. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: France deploys thousands of police amid a new wave of protests
articles.summary: Paris braced for a fresh march by students and workers over school funding and soaring living costs Saturday, one week after violent unrest left shops looted and cars burned. The new march was…

image.caption: Protesters hold placards on Saturday during an authorized demonstration organized by labour unions in Paris as part of nationwide protests against the rising cost of living. French high school and university students launched demonstrations earlier this month to protest against current education sta

blocks.text: World·New

Paris braced for a fresh march by students and workers over school funding and soaring living costs Saturday, one week after violent unrest left shops looted and cars burned. The new march was restricted to the city's southeastern edge, away from the centre, as police deployed in force across France.
Major museums, including the Louvre and Grand Palais, closed Saturday over protest-related concerns

Paris braced for a fresh march by students and workers over school funding and soaring living costs Saturday, one week after unrest left shops looted and cars burned. The new march was restricted to the city's southeastern edge as police deployed in force across France.

Scenes of looting, burned-out cars and attacks on public buildings left the impression that the government had lost control, as groups of masked vandals targeted businesses in Paris and other city centres.
Police imposed the new route Friday between Porte d'Italie and Porte de Vincennes, replacing the planned march from Bastille to Nation.

The movement began last month over staff shortages at one high school southeast of Paris. It now reaches well beyond the classroom. Students want more teachers, better school buildings and more university places. Unions are demanding higher wages and pensions to help people meet the cost of living.
‘It’s utter chaos': Protests in France evolve into anger over broader economy

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons. In central Paris, a few dozen gendarmes, or military police officers, were stationed beneath the Arc de Triomphe and along the nearby avenues.
A massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.
Museums are closed and shopkeepers are worried

Major museums, including the Louvre, Musée d'Orsay, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.

items: Tear gas, arrests and chaos as protests grip France

blocks.text: Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near the Saint-Lazare train station, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician's shop.
"I got the call last night," he said. "The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life."
Why thousands of high school students in France are protesting

Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged Parisian shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments is the responsibility of the government.
Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend.
Some protests have been banned

Protest marches are scheduled in Paris and Marseille, but some other rallies, including in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, have been banned by local authorities. In Lyon, French media reported that police used tear gas Saturday morning.

Cities outside Paris were hit hard by the unrest. Two suspects in the fire that nearly destroyed Limoges's 19th-century city hall were placed under formal investigation and held pending trial, French media reported. The probe includes attempted murder of a public official.
Tourist office in Lyon, France, set on fire
Trade unions have criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.

French President Emmanuel Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term, with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings.
French police move people away to prevent gatherings at the Place de la Bastille in Paris as part of nationwide protests that are taking place again on Saturday. (Dylan Martinez/Reuters)

Thousands of people gathered Saturday morning for an anti-far-right protest in the city of Orléans, about 110 kilometres south of Paris. It was organized on the sidelines of a two-day congress of Marine Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring's presidential election.
Students and workers are angry

Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system. Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.
They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros (around $313 Cdn) a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.

High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as unfair.

items: What's behind the youth protests in France? - Transcript

blocks.text: With the government seemingly unable to respond to students' demands, the movement has morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before the vote to choose Macron's successor.
"The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people," said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. "And it's not possible anymore."
Students in France clash with riot police amid weekslong education protests

articles.title: Additional 178 cases of measles reported by US health authorities amid outbreak
articles.summary:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 4,588 cases across the country, more than double the tally in 2025

Federal health authorities reported an additional 178 cases of measles…

blocks.text: Federal health authorities reported an additional 178 cases of measles in the US this week, as the vaccine-preventable illness continues to sicken people across at least 43 outbreaks.

The new data reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) comes as experts criticize the agency for lack of transparency, and as health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr takes steps to further upend US vaccine infrastructure.

The CDC reported 4,588 cases of measles across the country in 2026 as of Friday – more than double the tally for 2025. Pennsylvania alone reported 1,338 cases on the same day. The CDC also reported large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah, both of which are reporting more than 500 cases.

In spite of rising measles numbers, official tallies represent an undercount of the disease. Measles is widely regarded as one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine. Its most common symptoms – rash, runny nose, fever and cough – may not immediately send the infected to a doctor.

Measles sends one in five unvaccinated people who become infected to the hospital, and one to three people in 1,000 die of disease-related complications. The measles vaccine is 97% effective at preventing the disease. Vaccine side effects include injection-site soreness and low-grade fever. The measles vaccine has been a focal point of anti-vaccine activism for decades.

In Pennsylvania, which has had the worst outbreak in the nation for months, state authorities have reported five measles-associated deaths and are investigating a sixth. The CDC has reported three measles deaths nationally, but has refused to say where the third death took place, obscuring whether it is counting a death in Pennsylvania or elsewhere.
Kennedy reportedly asked senior CDC officials in September to remove a measles death from the official tally after he questioned whether the disease contributed to the death, according to Reuters.

In addition to criticism of how the CDC has tallied measles deaths, Health and Human Services (HHS) this week announced changes to vaccine injury reporting systems. A proposal will allow doctors to bill for reporting suspected vaccine injuries, among other changes.

The “vaccine adverse event reporting system”, or VAERS, has been a long-time fixation of the anti-vaccine movement. The system has proved useful for researchers tracking rare vaccine safety issues. However, it has also become a source of misinformation for anti-vaccine activists, who point to VAERS to make claims, however unfounded, about safety.

All vaccines have risks – a fact acknowledged by vaccinologists. Before Kennedy’s appointment to the health department, an expert panel considered each vaccine change individually to decide whether benefits outweigh risks. Kennedy fired all 17 sitting members of that board. He replaced them with members with whom he ideologically aligned. A court blocked the members’ appointment in March.

In his time as secretary, Kennedy also misleadingly claimed children get more than 90 vaccine doses; linked vaccines to autism in spite of extensive evidence to the contrary; directed the CDC to remove claims that vaccines do not cause autism from its website; claimed the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine contains “aborted fetal debris”; and stated that vitamin A and cod liver oil may help children with measles, which leading physicians described as misleading.

articles.title: Israelis are leaving the country in record numbers. Could a looming election accelerate the trend?
articles.summary: A record number of Israelis have left the country in resent years, data shows, and experts are raising the alarm ahead of a "watershed" election that they say could add to the trend and put more…

image.caption: Economist Itai Ater, seen in Tel Aviv in September, was the lead author of a study that found 99,000 Israelis left the country between January 2023 and December 2024. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)

blocks.text: World

A record number of Israelis have left the country in resent years, data shows, and experts are raising the alarm ahead of a "watershed" election that they say could add to the trend and put more strain on the country's economy.
A February study found 99,000 Israelis left the country in 2023 and 2024
Sitting at his desk in a sun-filled apartment in Tel Aviv, economist Itai Ater pored over data that shows more Israelis have left the country over the past three years than ever before.

Those have been tumultuous years for the country of around 10 million people, with war, economic uncertainty and a prime minister plagued by corruption charges whose trial started in 2020 and still hasn't reached a verdict.

Ater, a professor at the Coller School of Management at Tel Aviv University, says these departures could accelerate depending on the outcome of next week's legislative elections, destabilizing the country's economy and causing ripple effects throughout the region.

"Israelis are thinking, 'do I want to raise my kids in a country like this?'" Ater said. "Unfortunately, and I understand, I sympathize with their answers, many of them realize that the answer is no. And that's why they're leaving."

In February, Ater and his colleagues published a study using data collected from the Central Bureau of Statistics that found 99,000 Israelis left the country between January 2023 and December 2024. The study looked at Israelis who left for at least three consecutive months and stayed out of the country for more than 270 days during the first year of their departure.
Ater says he understands why people might want to leave: 'Israelis are thinking, "do I want to raise my kids in a country like this?"' (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)

According to the data, 50,000 left in 2023, a year that saw Hamas militants storm southern Israel, killing roughly 1,200 people and kidnapping another 250. Israel responded by embarking on a devastating military campaign in the Gaza Strip that continued until a fragile ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, though Israel still controls roughly 60 per cent of the enclave and engages in regular military activity there.
In 2024, 49,000 left. Ater says preliminary data shows the trend continued in 2025, and he believes the looming election could push those numbers even higher in 2026.
Election fuels uncertainty
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has been a defining figure in Israeli politics for the past three decades and is by far the country's longest serving leader, is once again vying for power.

Polls suggest his far-right bloc will fall short of the requisite 61 seats in the Knesset to form a government and that a rival bloc headed by Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, is currently in position to secure the most seats. As of now, Eisenkot's coalition is expected to be short of a majority.

items: Netanyahu's future uncertain as Israel starts to prepare for national election
Netanyahu faces fresh allegations he ignored warnings about Oct. 7 — right before an election

blocks.text: Israel's multiparty system, in which coalitions are often required in order to form a government, means the election results are often only just the beginning of the intrigue and lead to a jostling of parties and power in the days after the vote.
Netanyahu has long been considered a master at this process.

A supporter of Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party, displays a flag depicting him at Mahane Yehuda market, ahead of Israel's national election, in Jerusalem on Oct. 22. (Kevin Coombs/Reuters)

"We are really, really, really terrified in the sense that if there is no change in the patterns, then there's no change in October in the elections," Ater said. "These [emigration] numbers will go up dramatically."
Avigail Ben-Porat, 50, said she dreams of leaving but doesn't have the resources to do so.
The single mother lives in Kiryat Shmona, near the Israel-Lebanon border, where she said she still regularly hears the sound of rocket fire.

items: Israeli strikes on southern Lebanese town kill 12, including children, Health Ministry says

blocks.text: "I would go and never look back," Ben-Porat said. "Most of my friends are living abroad, some of them in Portugal, some of them moved to Canada. Some of them are in Thailand and in Goa in India. They pretty much left and fled."
Economic impact
It's not just the volume of people leaving that has Ater and others concerned — it's their jobs.

Ater's study suggests that 2023 and 2024 saw a dramatic increase in the number of doctors, Ph.D. holders and engineers leaving the country, with 2,360 net departures from Israeli engineers and 509 net departures from doctors.
"Israel's economy depends on the human capital," he said. "It's the tech industry, it's academia, it's health care. We need these best individuals to stay in Israel."
Lawyer Liam Schwartz, seen in Tel Aviv in September, says many companies, under pressure from investors, are moving chunks of their business outside Israel. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)
Liam Schwartz oversees the corporate immigration department at Goldfarb, Gross, Seligman, an Israeli law firm based in Tel Aviv. He said Israeli companies are also eying the exit.

"There are a good deal of Israeli companies that are just — they call it business viability," Schwartz said. "They have to answer to their shareholders who are not necessarily Israeli and investors who are not necessarily Israeli and they are concerned about the viability of business operations based in Israel. So they are more willing to move chunks of their workforce to North America or to Europe."
Schwartz believes the discontent started when the government proposed judicial reforms that would have stripped power away from the Supreme Court back in January 2023.

items: Israeli parliament approves key part of divisive judicial overhaul

blocks.text: "People are just disappointed," he said. "They feel like the Israeli government is no longer meeting its part of the social contract."
All of this adds up to making Tuesday's elections one of the country's most consequential.
"I think that the October elections in Israel are going to be a watershed moment in whether … the rate of Israeli emigration increases or not," Schwartz said.
For Ater, the stakes could not be higher.

"I'm saying it. It's a strategic concern, strategic risk," he said. "To the future of Israel as a democracy, as a liberal country, and that's not only a concern for Israel, it's also a concern for the Middle East and also for the world."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Willy Lowry is an award-winning correspondent for CBC News in Washington, D.C., where he provides breaking news and analysis across radio and television. Prior to that, he served as the senior U.S. correspondent at the National newspaper in D.C., where he covered the U.S. State Department, American foreign policy and its impacts on the Middle East and the wider world. Willy covered the Israel-Hamas war extensively, travelling to Israel and the occupied West Bank several times. He also covered the fall of ISIS in Syria. He started his career at CBC News in Montreal, where he worked his way up from intern to research assistant and eventually to video journalist.

articles.title: Will Guinea-Bissau remain trapped in political chaos?
articles.summary: Elections scheduled for December 6 in Guinea-Bissau have been postponed indefinitely. No new date has been set, leaving the country's return to civilian rule uncertain.

image.caption: Soldiers patrol the main street in Bissau, the capital of Guinea-Bissau. Following the 2025 military coup, the country's state institutions were suspendedImage: Luc Gnago/REUTERS

blocks.text: The parliamentary and presidential elections scheduled for December 6, 2026, in Guinea-Bissau will not take place as planned. Aly Silva, spokesperson for transitional Prime Minister Ilidio Vieira Te, confirmed to DW that the vote had been postponed until further notice. No new date has been set. The government first intends to discuss the matter in cabinet before publicly announcing when the elections will be held. It remains unclear whether they will take place in 2027 or not until 2028.

The country's political crisis dates back to November 26, 2025. Three days earlier, voters in Guinea-Bissau had elected a new parliament and president. Before the official results could be announced, the military seized power and halted the electoral process. Both then-President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and his challenger, Fernando Dias da Costa, had claimed victory. The military leadership promised a return to constitutional order.

blocks.caption: Guinea-Bissau's General Horta N'Tam (center) was sworn in as transitional leader and commander-in-chief on November 27, 2025Image: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP

blocks.text: For lawyer and political analyst Cabi Sanha, the postponement comes as no surprise. Since the coup, little has been done to create the conditions for credible elections, he says.
"The postponement was foreseeable," Sanha told DW. December 6 had indeed been set as the new election date. "But nothing was done to ensure that these elections could actually take place."
Political freedoms under pressure

The transitional government has justified the postponement by citing the lack of organizational and political conditions necessary for elections. The deadline for submitting candidacies had already passed on October 6. Political parties and potential candidates had not submitted their applications. According to the prime minister, the parties had also failed to hold congresses to select their candidates.

Sanha sees this as more than an organizational problem. He points to restrictions on political activities and the lack of dialogue with key actors in the electoral process. Political parties and civil society have not been sufficiently involved, he says. Mediation efforts by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and Senegal have so far failed to produce a solution.
"Free, transparent and inclusive elections are only possible if the necessary conditions are established beforehand," the lawyer says.

He therefore also views the parties' failure to nominate candidates as a consequence of the political environment. "How are parties supposed to nominate candidates when political activities are restricted in the country? They cannot hold party congresses or organize rallies."

blocks.caption: The funeral of human rights activist Vigario Balanta in Bissau, Guinea-Bissau. His body was found on March 31, bearing signs of torture, in a swamp outside the capitalImage: DW

blocks.text: Leading opposition figures are also staying abroad. Domingos Simoes Pereira, head of the main opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), was allowed to travel to Portugal in July 2026 for medical treatment after being released from detention. He had previously been held in pretrial detention in connection with an investigation into an alleged coup attempt. His defense team denies the allegations and has criticized the proceedings as politically motivated.
The absence of key opposition figures and restrictions on political organizing are making it harder to conduct an electoral process intended to pave the way for a return to civilian government.
An election date without a timetable

What happens next remains unclear. Government spokesperson Aly Silva says the transitional government will first discuss the matter in cabinet. Only afterward will a new election date be announced publicly. So far, there is no concrete timetable.

It is therefore also unclear when political parties will be able to complete their internal selection procedures, nominate candidates and begin campaigning. For Sanha, this is another indication that there is still insufficient evidence of the political will needed to restore constitutional order.
"I do not believe that logistical problems are the main issue. Rather, there appears to be a lack of political will to move the electoral process forward," he says.
Dispute over the constitution

The political crisis has been compounded by a controversial constitutional reform. In a referendum on August 30, 2026, voters approved constitutional amendments that expand the president's powers and reduce the size of parliament from 102 to 65 seats. Critics question the legitimacy of the process because the reform was prepared under military rule and without a regularly elected parliament. The opposition had called for a boycott of the vote.

Fernando Vaz, spokesperson for the National Transitional Council, defends the changes. He says the process was not a comprehensive rewriting of the constitution but a targeted revision. The reform is intended to help overcome the country's political instability, he argues.

"The constitution must be one of the instruments that lead our country toward greater stability," Vaz told DW. The transitional period had provided an opportunity to amend provisions that, in the military leadership's view, were obstructing the country's political development.

Vaz also rejects criticism that the reform gives the president additional powers at the expense of the prime minister. "The president of the republic is the head of state, while the prime minister is the head of government," he emphasizes.

Critics see it differently. The new constitutional framework strengthens the presidency: the president is to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and the government and, under certain conditions, dissolve parliament. At the same time, the number of parliamentary seats is being reduced. It remains disputed whether the reform will genuinely contribute to stability or instead concentrate more power in the presidency.

blocks.caption: Around 70 percent of valid votes in a constitutional referendum on August 30, 2026, were cast in favor of constitutional amendmentsImage: DW

blocks.text: Local elections are not enough

The transitional government has announced plans to hold local elections in 2027. Sanha broadly welcomes the proposal: Guinea-Bissau has never held such elections since independence. Nevertheless, he stresses that they must not replace the outstanding national elections.
"First, parliamentary and presidential elections must take place so that the country can return to constitutional order. Local elections can follow afterward," he says.

Local elections cannot compensate for the lack of democratic legitimacy at the national level. Political freedoms must also be restored so that parties can select their candidates and voters can genuinely choose between political alternatives.
A Transition With No Clear End
Guinea-Bissau has endured decades of political instability, marked by military coups, institutional crises and repeated interruptions of democratic processes. The latest coup continues this pattern.

The renewed postponement of the elections shows how far the country remains from a return to constitutional order. Setting a new election date alone will not be enough. Political activities must be permitted again, parties must be included in the process, and reliable conditions for elections must be established, lawyer Cabi Sanha told DW.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: No unions, low taxes: why some of Britain’s top chefs are opening outposts in Gulf states
articles.summary:
Leading restaurateur says Gulf countries actively help businesses set up, while east Asia has a better work ethic

Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a…

blocks.text: Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur.
James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf.

Other restaurants have opened in Dubai, including the celebrity hotspot Scott’s in Mayfair, the two Michelin-starred Indian venue Gymkhana, and the upmarket Chinese restaurant Park Chinois. Isabel’s, a Mayfair institution enjoyed by politicians, has opened in Abu Dhabi. And the trendy Borough Market bakery Bread Ahead has branched out in Dubai.

Despite conflicts in the Middle East, including the US-Israeli war in Iran which caused Dubai to face bombardment and an exodus of expats earlier this year, restaurants continue to open in the emirate.

Speaking from Hong Kong, where he is looking at opportunities in Asia, Robson said: “East Asia, the States and the Gulf are key growth targets for us. America champions business, the Gulf actively encourages and assists, whilst east Asia has a work ethic and taxation system that puts the UK to shame. I’m incredibly keen to start working in these regions over the next few years.”
Fallow has risen to fame partially through Instagram, where it has 650,000 followers, and its striking dishes including a whole cod’s head drenched in a spicy butter sauce.

Restaurateurs have complained of the VAT rate for hospitality in the UK, which at 20% is one of the highest rates in Europe. The European average for restaurants is about 12%. In Italy, it is set at 10% for food sold in restaurants. Chefs are calling for Andy Burnham to use next week’s budget to cut the VAT rate.

blocks.caption: Two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of several London establishments that has opened in Dubai  Photograph: Sophia Evans/The Observer

blocks.text: “We have had a tsunami of taxes that have got to the point where taking business risk simply does not make sense in the UK,” Robson said, “Sadly the country has sleepwalked into multiple anti-growth taxations the last two budgets and likely more will be forthcoming next week.”
The entrepreneur has asked for VAT to be put more in line with Europe. “Add 25% corporation tax and 40%-plus dividend tax, then you start to question why do businesses any more.”
Jason Atherton, a Michelin-starred chef, spends a third of his time at his Dubai restaurant now and says it is easier to make a profit abroad than in London.

But human rights experts have warned of exploitation and poor worker protections in the Gulf. Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s director of campaigns, said: “Dubai might look like an attractive place to do business, but the UAE has a very poor record on workers’ rights and protection from labour exploitation. The UAE has spent heavily on polishing its image in the UK, not least through Manchester City, but that glamour shouldn’t distract from how the people who keep its economy running are treated.
after newsletter promotion

“Migrant workers, who make up the majority of the UAE’s population, remain bound by a sponsorship system that ties them to their employers and exposes them to labour abuse. They are denied the right to form trade unions, leaving them few ways to challenge unfair treatment.

“Any UK business expanding into the Gulf has a responsibility to carry out proper human rights due diligence, to make sure the people working in its kitchens are treated fairly, paid properly and able to raise concerns without fear of losing their job or visa.”

blocks.caption: The British Michelin-starred chef Jason Atherton has previously spoken out about high taxes and the UK’s struggling hospitality sector. Photograph: Richard Saker/The Guardian

blocks.text: Some restaurants in Dubai are struggling: Dinner by Heston is temporarily closed and has been since the fallout from the war in the Middle East. The Michelin guide came under fire earlier this month because it included 16 restaurants that were either permanently or temporarily closed. It appears that some visits were undertaken by inspectors at the beginning of the year, before the war started.

Robson said he had no resentment paying UK tax. “I am incredibly proud of the taxes I pay and feel privileged that I can contribute to our country’s deficit and will continue to do so,” he said. “My point is UK growth simply does not have any risk-reward balance any more, therefore it’s play incredibly safe here and focus overseas.”

articles.title: From horses to electric cars: Sask. couple sees world transform over 75-year marriage
articles.summary: Helen and Larry Frey of Fort Qu'Appelle, Sask., have not only witnessed growth in their relationship, but growth in the world around them over the quarter-century of their marriage.

image.caption: Larry and Helen Frey have been together since they were 21 and 22 years old. (Janani Whitfield/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
Helen and Larry Frey of Fort Qu'Appelle, Sask., have not only witnessed growth in their relationship, but growth in the world around them over the quarter-century of their marriage.
Helen and Larry Frey celebrate milestone anniversary this month
Larry and Helen Frey figure no one else had a wedding night quite like theirs.
On that chilly November night in 1951, they came home to a rugged prairie house with no cupboards or electricity.
"We had to take our bed apart, bring it out where this cookstove was. You light a fire and get everything warmed up," said Larry, who's now 96. "That's how tough life was."
Their love and sense of humour is still burning strong 75 years later. Helen, 97, has a big chuckle recalling that frosty wedding night.
"I thought it was great," she laughs.
"Nobody has that story to tell, [that] they had to take their bed apart and put it beside the kitchen stove before they could have sex that night. What the heck!"

Life's challenges clearly did not deter the. The Freys are now celebrating a huge milestone at their home in Fort Qu'Appelle, Sask.: a wedding anniversary marking three-quarters of a century together.
Helen, left, and Larry Frey remember having to do everything for themselves: growing their own food, building their own barn and home, and farming to make their living. (Submitted by Cheryl Lendvoy)
They've seen huge changes in the world, from farming with horses and having no phones to zipping across the country in an electric car and Facetiming their children on cell phones.
They first met when he was 21 and she was 22.
"I married an older woman because I was told they were more fun," Larry jokes.
Helen was working as a clerk at a store when she made up her mind about getting to know Larry. They hadn't even met at that point, but she'd heard he was a caring man, she says.
"So when I first saw him walk in the store, I thought, 'Oh my God, I chose him, and how funny-looking he is and how young he is.'"
Larry says he noticed her figure immediately.
"She still looks the same," he adds.
Biggest changes in their lifetime
Farming was hard work. Larry says things changed drastically over the years, from using literal horse power with a team of horses and threshing machines, to using high-powered machines.
He's always been crazy about cars, and even now, he still picks the best. Larry's eyes grow big with excitement when he talks about driving his electric car.
Larry and Helen Frey in their electric vehicle on a Saskatchewan highway. (Submitted by Cheryl Lendvoy)
Growing up, there were hardly any paved roads. For their early dates, the couple often went on horseback.
Electricity made the biggest change in their lifetime.

"[You] didn't have to go down the cellar to get something to eat," Larry recalls. "A refrigerator, a block heater on a car. You didn't have to light a fire under the damn thing. These were big changes."

Another big change was in the people around them: four children, 10 grandkids, 16 great-grandkids and even one great-great-grandchild. Family and friends will all join them this month to celebrate their exciting milestone.
Larry and Helen Frey on their wedding day 75 years ago. (Submitted by Cheryl Lendvoy)
Do they have tips on how to stay happily married?
Larry's advice is short and to the point: "Button your lip."
Sometimes the best thing in a relationship is to give your partner space, he says.
Helen says she isn't qualified to give advice.

"The years just go by and you keep on living life," she says, noting that over the course of their relationship, they've shared amazing moments of joy but also hardships and tragedy. They've met all of it together.
"Live every day as you find it," she says, looking over to her husband.
"I just look at him and think, 'Oh God, he's mine.' And I'm so thankful."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Randi LaRocque is a Métis woman working as a reporter with CBC Saskatchewan. She can be reached at randi.larocque@cbc.ca

articles.title: House prosecution submitted formal offer of evidence vs Sara Duterte - Barbers
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Saturday confirmed that it had filed its formal offer of evidence in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, days before the October 23 deadline.

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 6:39pm
The House prosecution panel on Saturday confirmed that it had filed its formal offer of evidence in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, days before the October 23 deadline.

“We already filed ‘yung ating formal offer of evidence. Kung hindi ako nagkakamali, Miyerkoles. This is days before the deadline,” House prosecution spokesperson Robert Ace Barbers said at a news forum.
(We already filed our formal offer of evidence on Wednesday, if I’m not mistaken.)
Barbers said the defense would have 10 days to comment on the prosecution’s formal offer before the Senate impeachment court rules on the admissibility of the evidence.

He said the formal offer included all documentary evidence and witness testimonies presented by the prosecution in support of Article 2 of the impeachment complaint, which alleges that Duterte accumulated unexplained wealth through assets not declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).
Barbers expressed confidence that the prosecution could secure a conviction.

“Honestly, ang pakiramdam namin, we are confident that we can secure a conviction. Bakit? Doon po sa aming mga nailatag na ebidensiya, matibay at malakas po ang aming paniwala na itong mga ebidensiyang ito ay sumusuporta sa aming alegasyon na merong hindi maipaliwanag na yaman ang ating Pangalawang Pangulo. At merong mga nalabag na probisyon sa Saligang Batas at merong nalabag na mga batas ang ating Pangalawang Pangulo,” he said.

(Honestly, we are confident that we can secure a conviction. Why? Based on the evidence we have presented, we firmly believe that it supports our allegation that the Vice President has unexplained wealth and has violated provisions of the Constitution and other laws.)
The House prosecution panel had initially been allotted 62 trial days to present its evidence but used only 39 days before resting its case on October 13.

The panel had earlier dropped three other articles of impeachment: Article 1, which concerned confidential funds; Article 3, which alleged bribery; and Article 4, which accused Duterte of making grave threats against President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. and his family. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm
articles.summary: The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far…

image.caption: In a bid to help farmers, the EU has proposed unlimited, open-ended approval for certain pesticidesImage: Andrii Yalanskyi/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.
Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.
Why does the EU want to deregulate pesticides?
The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.
In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances."
But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.
The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."
Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation."
He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.
How do pesticides affect human health, environment?
Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.
Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

blocks.caption: In January 2020, beekeepers in Berlin protested the continued authorization of glyphosate by leaving unsellable tainted honey at the entrance to Germany's Agriculture MinistryImage: Adam Berry/Getty Images

blocks.text: When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides."

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.
"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.
More than 50 substances banned since 2011

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.
"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.
That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.
Pesticides banned in Europe linked to bees deaths in Kenya
Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.
Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.
"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said.
Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.
Farmers need 'incentive' to switch to safer pesticides

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.
Can we cut down on pesticide use with 'plant vaccines'?

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's important to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet."

articles.title: British woman dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea in the Bahamas
articles.summary: The children were subsequently rescued from the water, police say.

blocks.text: In a statement, posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.

"Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
"Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
"In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
"She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered.
"Foul play is not suspected at this time.
"An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death."
A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

articles.title: Seven missing after multi-storey building collapses in Kenya's capital
articles.summary: Rescue efforts are under way to find people trapped under the block, which was still under construction when it buckled.

blocks.text: A search and rescue effort is under way to find seven people feared trapped under rubble after a building collapsed in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.
Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets.

Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops that had opened at the base of the building.
The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.

The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.

Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.

Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.

articles.title: British woman dies trying to save sons on Bahamas snorkelling trip
articles.summary:
The 36-year-old died after two boys reportedly swept away by strong current near Bimini, police say

A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a…

blocks.text: A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling.
The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday.
The force said they believed she was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island of Bimini when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
The police said that in an attempt to rescue her boys, “the woman was also swept away”. The children were later rescued from the water.
The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support.
Bimini is a small island between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland.
The island is best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and is also home to a world-leading shark research centre.

In a statementposted on social media, the Royal Bahamas police force said: “According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini ferry dock.

“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
“She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. Foul play is not suspected at this time.”
An autopsy would be carried out to help determine the exact cause of death, the statement said.
A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”

articles.title: Kim Jong-un crosses over newly opened bridge into China
articles.summary:
Visit by train over New Yalu River Bridge marks North Korean leader’s first known trip abroad in more than a year

Kim Jong-un has travelled to China over a newly opened bridge marking the…

blocks.text: Kim Jong-un has travelled to China over a newly opened bridge marking the North Korean leader’s first known trip abroad in more than a year, South Korean officials have said.

A government source told the Yonhap news agency on Saturday that Kim had arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong, in Liaoning province, after taking a train from Pyongyang to Sinuiju and crossing the New Yalu River Bridge.
Yonhap also reported that the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, had travelled to the city. Kim’s trip was not announced in advance and had not been confirmed by Pyongyang or Beijing by Saturday evening.
China will mark the anniversary on Sunday of its entry into the 1950-53 Korean war on the North’s side.

Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum devoted to China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.
Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.

The 3km bridge opened in mid-October, 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.

blocks.caption: The New Yalu River Bridge seen from the Chinese border city of Dandong, in Liaoning province. Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters

blocks.text: The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June, his first trip there in seven years.

Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.
Xi will host the Apec summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.
Reuters reported on Friday, however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.

articles.title: Hundreds of protests expected across France, with shops, businesses and tourist sites closed – Europe live
articles.summary:
France will deploy 70,000 officers around the country. Protests are also expected in Italy, Spain, Austria, Portugal, Albania and Ireland

All through the night in neighbourhoods in…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 15m agoOpening summary

blocks.caption: Angelique Chrisafis

blocks.text: Angelique Chrisafis

blocks.caption: A jogger runs past a Societe Generale bank branch with its storefronts protected by wooden panels on the Champs-Elysees avenue in Paris ahead of nationwide protests onOctober 24, 2026.  Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

blocks.text: All through the night in neighbourhoods in the centre and east of Paris, the sound of sawing, drilling and hammering rang out as wooden boards were hastily secured into place to cover windows and shop-fronts.
Businesses being boarded up included opticians, supermarkets and pharmacies as well as trainers and handbag stores.
Hundreds of shops were smashed and looted over two nights last weekend in Paris, and thousands more in cities across France, including Marseille and Bordeaux.
At a public meeting at Paris city hall this week, some shop-owners had cried as they spoke of their fears of businesses being smashed and looted again this weekend.

“I’m afraid there isn’t enough wooden board left to protect shops and the demand is making it so expensive to board up shops,” one optician near Châtelet in the city centre said. “We’ll close up and take all our stock of glasses out of the shop.”

blocks.caption: Workers install wooden panels to protect the windows of the gaming club Partouche Pasino Club in Paris  Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

blocks.text: Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of events in Europe – we will be closely following protests across the continent today.

In France, hundreds of thousands are expected at rallies across the country, with high school students, unionists, “yellow vest” demonstrators and others turning out for a fourth weekend of protests demanding more government funding for schools and measures to help with housing and the cost of living.

Desperate to avoid the looting and property damage seen on the fringes of some protests last weekend, French authorities have ramped up restrictions on where protesters can march and which groups are “authorised” to do so. They’ve increased policing 20%, mobilising 70,000 police officers and soldiers to the streets, including both elite units and trainee officers.
Many of Paris’s metro stations and major museums and tourist sites are shut today, while across the country, shops and businesses have been urged to close their doors.

Community tensions are also high following a deadly shooting on Friday west of Paris where the gunman targeted non-white people, killing one person and injuring five others including a child. The French president called it a “racist terrorist attack”.

Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s anti-immigration party is also due to hold its national conference in the central city of Orléans. The far-right National Rally’s meeting is expected to draw up to 30,000 counter-demonstrators.
Protests are also being held in Italy, Spain, Austria, Portugal, Albania and Ireland today.
Stay with us for all the developments.

articles.title: Can millions of people live on the moon? These scientists say yes — but not for very long
articles.summary: Billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos are claiming that we can expect big cities with millions of people on the moon, but a new study found that that may not be possible, so don’t start packing…

image.caption: This artist’s rendering depicts astronauts, habitats, rovers, power systems and cargo operations supporting sustained human activities at NASA's Moon Base near the lunar South Pole. A recent study found that while a small population of humans can live on the moon, a large city of one million people

blocks.text: Science·New

Billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos are claiming that we can expect big cities with millions of people on the moon, but a new study found that that may not be possible, so don’t start packing just yet.
Power and water are the main resources needed to live on the moon
Humans have long dreamed about reaching out and exploring space. Most science fiction, more often than not, portrays cities on the dusty lunar surface and Mars.
And if you listen to some billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, cities on the moon are coming soon.
In fact, in February, SpaceX CEO Musk posted on social media that the company was shifting its focus away from settling on Mars — something Musk has been passionate about for the past decade.

“For those unaware, SpaceX has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years,” he wrote.

For those unaware, SpaceX has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the Moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years. The mission of SpaceX remains the same: extend consciousness and life as we know it to the stars. It is only possible to travel to Mars when the planets align every 26 months (six month trip time), whereas we can launch to the Moon every 10 days (2 day trip time). This means we can iterate much faster to complete a Moon city than a Mars city. That said, SpaceX will also strive to build a Mars city and begin doing so in about 5 to 7 years, but the overriding priority is securing the future of civilization and the Moon is faster.—elonmusk

This statement — and those of Blue Origin CEO Bezos, who has claimed “millions of people” will be living in space by 2045 — intrigued Martin Elvis, senior astrophysicist at Harvard University’s Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory.
He, along with astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell, honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre in England, decided to take a look at the numbers.
But their findings, it turns out, aren't great for a lunar civilization, so don’t start packing just yet.
In their paper, published in the journal Frontiers in Space Technologies, the pair decided to examine power and water needed to sustain humans on the moon.
When it comes to power, they found that solar and nuclear would be enough to sustain one million people on the lunar surface.
But then there's water.
It may be surprising to some, but there is water on the moon. It’s believed that most of it is contained in permanently shadowed regions (PSR), areas at the poles that never see sunlight.
But in this study, they found that there’s not enough on the moon to sustain a large human presence on the lunar surface.
NASA shares plans for moon base

“Our work shows that, yeah, if you want to have an Antarctic base on the moon for the next few hundred years, no problem. If you want to have a small town, that's doable. If you want to cover the face of the moon with cities, like in the best science fiction, then you have to find a way to get the water there, because it's not there right now,” McDowell said.

Assuming that there is roughly one billion tonnes of water on the moon, which is in line with current estimates, they found that a civilization of one million people would only be able to live on the moon for roughly 100 years. And that’s only if we can recycle 98 per cent of the water, which is what is done on the International Space Station.
'A small lake'
Elvis said that while one billion tonnes of water sounds like a lot, you have to put it in perspective.

“If you had a huge aquarium the size of Central Park in Manhattan, you could fill it up to where the Statue of Liberty was just underwater and that's the amount of water you've got. So it's huge in one way, but … it's a small lake. And a small lake is not going to supply a big city for very long.”
That’s not to say that humans can’t ever live on the moon. If it were a town of 10,000, they found that would be sustainable for centuries.
However, that's assuming that the one billion tonnes of water is an accurate estimate.
"Very likely a billion is way overestimating. It's probably 20 or 30 times too big," Elvis said.
How Artemis II is setting up the next stage of space exploration
He also said that it's unlikely that we'd be able to recover all the water that's available. Instead, it would be more like one-third to half of what is present.
"So my best guess is the real amount of water available that we can be fairly confident about is one per cent of what we said before. So instead of 100 years, it's one year."
And there's one other thing: We don't know in what form that water exists. And we need to figure that out.

items: We’ve already been to the moon, so why are we going again?
NASA has set its sights on a moon base. Here's how Canada can play an important role

blocks.text: "It's one thing to detect it from satellites, but ... there are uncertainties in those measurements," said Gordon Osinski, a professor in planetary geology at Western University in London, Ont.

"I think it is there, but let's go and ground-truth that and confirm it. And then there's the bigger unknowns of what form it's in…. Is it more like the permafrost up in the Arctic, where it's basically soil with, you know, sub-millimetre size ice crystals, which are hard to get out of?"
While this may sound like pessimistic news for humanity's plans to explore the cosmos, McDowell said it's best to know what you're dealing with.
"The truth is never negative," he said. "What's negative is to actually go and try and do something that isn't going to work."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science. You can send her story ideas at nicole.mortillaro@cbc.ca.

articles.title: 82 days later, no repairs started on washed-out road dividing small Quebec town
articles.summary: Residents in L’Ascension, Que., are still waiting on repairs after August flooding washed away part of their main road. The municipality's mayor blames the delay for repairs on the bureaucracy of…

image.caption: L'Ascension Mayor Jacques Allard points to white spray paint monitoring the ongoing erosion of Principale Street. (Andie Bennett/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal

Residents in L’Ascension, Que., are still waiting on repairs after August flooding washed away part of their main road. The municipality's mayor blames the delay for repairs on the bureaucracy of different levels of government.
L’Ascension, Que., mayor blames delays on bureaucracy of different levels of government
Mayor Jacques Allard stands in front of the 70-foot gap that now divides his town of L’Ascension.
Spray painted white lines on the ground track the ongoing erosion that continues with every rainfall.
It's been 82 days since heavy rain washed away parts of Principale Street and de L’Ascension Road that connects the small municipality to the city of Rivière-Rouge on Aug. 3.
The mayor says on its end, L’Ascension is ready to start work to repair the road.

They have their contractor, the engineer plans are in place and the replacement culvert — twice the diameter of the previous one — is sitting idly by the protective fencing that surrounds the giant crater.
So what's the delay?

items: Situation in L'Ascension, Que., 'stable' after municipality declares state of emergency

blocks.text: The municipality says it's waiting for the green light from the Quebec government to begin the repair, which their contractor expects to take five weeks and cost roughly $3 million.
A report of the required work also had to be sent to Fisheries and Oceans Canada for approval — a report that took 70 days to be approved and was then sent to the government.
The washout is directly in front of the fire hall, impacting emergency services. (Andie Bennett/CBC)
L’Ascension is now awaiting confirmation that they will receive the subsidy from the program that provides financial support to municipalities affected by natural disasters.
Allard says the bureaucracy slowing down this work is unacceptable.
“Normally they have a protocol to fast track. Now it is a very slow track," he said.
300 people cut off
The crater left behind by the rushing water that ripped up sections of asphalt and collapsed culverts is 45 feet deep and 70 feet wide.
Thirty per cent of the small population lives on the other side of the gap, meaning around 300 people are cut off from their community.
Nicolas Côté owns a small grocery store in town. He says business is already down 15 per cent compared to last year due to its inaccessibility.
Residents on the other side of the gap must either take their business to the nearby town of Rivière-Rouge or make a detour of more than an hour to reach their local grocery store.
The gap is 45 feet deep and 70 feet wide and sits where the road used to connect in L’Ascension. (Andie Bennett/CBC)
Côté says when you live in a small town where the population is just shy of 1,000 people, it's more like a family.
He says many people have sent him messages saying they hope the repairs happen soon so they will see him again and be able to shop at their local store.
“Maybe it's tough to fix, but to wait so much time … and we still don't know what will happen," Côté said.
The local grocery store in L’Ascension has already seen a 15 per cent drop in business compared to last year due to the lack of access for residents. (Andie Bennett/CBC)
With winter coming, Allard says there is a lot of anxiety within the community. He is also concerned about the financial impact if the repairs are not completed as soon as possible.

“On the other side, it takes five minutes to get here. Now it's 50 minutes. How will we pay to remove the snow in the winter? The trucks will have to make this detour. We will have a big expense for fuel," he said.

CBC News reached out to the Domestic Security Ministry for comment. It said it is currently reviewing the file and will confirm, as soon as possible, whether the work is eligible for financial assistance.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Andie Bennett is a journalist covering Quebec's Laurentians and Lanaudière regions. Andie lives in Morin-Heights, Que., and has an office space in Piedmont. She can be reached at andie.bennett@cbc.ca
