articles.title: Why a new round in the U.S.-Iran conflict could be the most devastating yet
articles.summary: As the U.S. midterm elections approach, intelligence analysts warn that the United States and Israel are preparing for a devastating third round of direct military conflict with Iran. Experts caution…

image.caption: Iranian missiles are displayed next to a banner with a picture of Iranain Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, on a street in Tehran on Sept. 27. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency via REUTERS)

blocks.text: The warning signs are flashing red with indications that once the ballots are counted in the U.S. midterm elections, the United States and Israel will relaunch their war with Iran.
The next round of attacks could be more devastating than the first, warn analysts.

"A renewed war seems almost inevitable," said Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli Middle East and Iran analyst whose earlier warnings and cautions about the risks of a direct conflict with Iran were largely borne out by events.

Citrinowicz, who worked for Israel's military as an intelligence official for more than two decades, had initially warned that any U.S. and Israeli attack on the Islamic regime would not likely lead to regime change but would instead end up engulfing the entire region in a wider conflict — an assessment that proved true.
In an interview with CBC News, he said that assessment still holds.
"The problem is there is no silver bullet solution to the impasse we are now at in the Persian Gulf and in front of Trump he has only bad and worse options."

Under U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, their countries broke with decades of restraint and shadow warfare and launched two distinct wars with Iran over the past 18 months.
Iranian women look at a building, which was damaged in a U.S. and Israeli strike in March, in Tehran on Aug. 22. (Reuters)
The first in June 2025 began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, lasted 12 days and ended with a fragile ceasefire.

The conflict roared back to life in February of this year following a massive U.S. military buildup in the region. It began with Israel's strikes against Iran's senior leadership, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Worst round yet
Citrinowicz, who's with Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, said a third round of war could be the worst yet, based on what Iranian officials are telegraphing.

"They will attack the energy facilities in the Gulf. But more than that, they will cause significant damage to civilian infrastructure, communications, as well as cutting off the internet lines going under [the] Hormuz Strait," he said.
He said there is even a possibility that Iran could push some of its massive land army into the fight with limited assaults against Gulf countries that house U.S. bases, such as Kuwait and Bahrain.
"We'll see a regional war with Iran investing a lot in attacking the U.S. presence in the region to cause maximum economical damage to the U.S. international economy."

Smoke rises from a burning vessel, following what the U.S. Central Command said was a strike on an Iranian-affiliated dhow, at a location given as the Gulf of Oman, in this still image taken from a video released on Oct. 14. (U.S. Central Command/Reuters)
Midterm dynamics

While both sides have largely avoided fresh strikes against each other's bases or territory since the summer truce collapsed, the conflict remains active. The U.S. imposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports and Iran has continued to target commercial shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, driving up global energy costs.

Posting on Truth Social Thursday, Trump blamed Iran for trying to artificially drive up oil prices ahead of the midterms on Nov. 3, elections that many pollsters believe will see Trump's Republicans lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as well.
"They are even making up fake hits, mines and everything else," said Trump, implying that Iran is exaggerating the extent of the damage it's causing.

A report published this week by the Washington, D.C.,-based Critical Threats Project alongside the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) also suggested Iran is trying to use strikes on shipping to weaken Trump's position heading into the elections.

"The increase in Iranian attacks on vessels is part of the ongoing Iranian campaign to pressure the United States to meet Iranian demands, including control over the Strait, by driving up global prices," the report said.
People walk on the beach, with vessels in the Strait of Hormuz visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Oct. 13. (Razieh Poudat West Asia News Agency/Reuters)
Iran's demands

Iran's government wants relief from punishing sanctions, reparations for the damage caused by earlier U.S.-Israel strikes, the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets and the right to keep its supplies of enriched uranium.
Mediators with Pakistan and Qatar have spent weeks trying to push diplomatic solutions to get the two sides talking again, but to no avail.
For both Netanyahu and Trump, the war with Iran remains unfinished business.

items: Iran says 7 ships have been struck in Strait of Hormuz, Saudis intercept drones in airspace
Iran's president says country won't surrender after Trump threat to 'annihilate' Islamic republic

blocks.text: The Islamic regime not only remains in power, but its leadership has also proven remarkably adept at adapting to both the military strikes and the economic blockade imposed by the West.

"The war in some respects has probably persuaded Iran's leadership to double down on their commitment to the revolutionary ideology that has really forged this regime," said Suzanne Maloney, a vice-president and director of the foreign policy program at the Washington, D.C.,-based Brookings Institution.
Like Citroniwicz, she said if war resumes, Trump won't be able to easily contain it.
"The retaliation as we've seen will come not just from Iran, but from its proxies and partners in the region," she said, referring to the Houthi militias in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Iran's goal won't just be to hit back at U.S. military targets but also soft economic targets, such as airports, that could undermine Gulf countries for years to come, she said.
How the Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict plays into broader Middle East war
Maloney and Karim Sadjadpour, a prominent Iran expert with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, were speaking on an online Carnegie panel about the future of the war in Iran.
"I genuinely don't think that President Trump has a clear idea in his head what he's trying to achieve," said Sadjadpour.
"I don't see any possibility of what Trump is looking for — which is like a knockout punch, a military strike — which will essentially force the Iranians into a compromise or capitulation."
Nuclear timeline?
Trump claimed his justification for the initial attacks on Iran was to ensure the country doesn't get a nuclear weapon.

At the time, while Iran possessed enough enriched uranium to theoretically pursue a weapon, many independent experts and U.S. intelligence sources believed it was still likely months away from doing so — and perhaps more importantly, that the regime's supreme leader had not yet made the definitive political decision to cross the nuclear threshold.
Since those initial June 2025 strikes, the human cost of the war has been severe.
Western NGOs claim the death toll in Iran is well over 7,000, including civilians and government figures who have been killed in the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes.
Lebanon has also suffered an especially heavy toll, with local media reporting more than 4,000 fatalities.
Twenty-one U.S. service members were killed, mostly by Iranian strikes on U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf, while more than 70 Israelis have died.
People drive near a billboard depicting U.S. President Donald Trump on a building in Tehran on Sept. 16. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters)
There have also been deaths throughout the Gulf countries, including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, as well as in Iraq and Yemen.
The New York Times and other U.S. media are reporting the Pentagon is working on a new battle plan for the possible next round of attacks — but whether Trump will ultimately authorize it is unknown.
'Finishing the job'
Israel's leadership, on the other hand, has made no secret of its push to restart the conflict, with Netanyahu explicitly stating his desire to bring down the Iran regime by "finishing the job."
Netanyahu faces Israeli voters in the coming days, and whether he hangs onto his job could end up in a photo finish.

items: Netanyahu faces fresh allegations he ignored warnings about Oct. 7 — right before an election

blocks.text: Relaunching the war with Iran could offer him a tactical way to stay in power; even if his party loses seats, a widening security crisis could lead to the creation of an emergency unity government with members of the opposition, said Citrinowicz.

"The real risk is that Netanyahu will involve his political considerations together with some other operational development in Iran that he is going to not necessarily invent, but probably [inflate]," he said.
A shopkeeper works at his shop in a local market in Tehran on Sept. 26. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency/Reuters)
"And this combination will lead to an unnecessary attack against Iran."
Sadjadpour from the Carnegie panel said there is no obvious military way out of the impasse and says Trump's maximalist goals have closed down diplomatic options as well.

"I believe there's a pretty clear formula under which it [Iran's government] compromises," said Sadjadpour. "It's when it faces what I would describe as existential economic pressure, coupled with a clear, limited diplomatic exit.
"If you're asking them to change their identity, that's not going to succeed."

articles.title: Nature vs. bulldozers: The environment minister's balancing act at UN nature summit
articles.summary: Canada is showing up at this year's international nature summit in Armenia with pledges to protect swaths of land bigger than most countries. But it's also facing criticism for advancing major…

image.caption: Canada's Environment, Climate Change and Nature Minister Julie Dabrusin is heading to Armenia for a major biodiversity conference. (Patrick Doyle/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics

Canada is showing up at this year's international nature summit in Armenia with pledges to protect swaths of land bigger than most countries. But it's also facing criticism for advancing major projects that put those protections in jeopardy.
Julie Dabrusin heads to COP17 in Armenia looking for ways for Canada to have 'leadership role'

Environment and Climate Change Minister Julie Dabrusin spoke to CBC News about the work she hopes to advance in Yerevan and responded to critics who say the government's actions on the nature file are "incoherent."
Dabrusin is heading to COP17, the United Nations biodiversity conference, on Saturday.
"Canada is the second-largest country in the world. We have the longest coastline in the world. So whatever we do has a real global impact," said Dabrusin before departing to Armenia.

items: Biologists seek justice for forgotten kingdom of fungi

blocks.text: She said international environmental conferences are "real moments" for Canada to have a "leadership role" in "pushing the world" to protect nature and reduce global emissions.
The environment minister attends COP17 on the heels of making a series of announcements to conserve lands and waters.
In October, Dabrusin announced that Canada is conserving an area of forest and peatlands near Kapuskasing, Ont., that's 1.3 times the size of Toronto.

In 2025, the minister said Ottawa would support the conservation of an area of land that's the size of Japan. As part of the initiative Northwest Territories: Our Land for the Future, the Canadian government is funding one of the world's largest Indigenous-led projects, conserving 380,000 square kilometres of land and water.
Policy 'incoherence': Greenpeace
But Dabrusin's attendance at COP17 comes as the Carney government receives sustained criticism for changes it's making to Canada's environmental laws.
"I think the big headline specifically for Canada is policy incoherence," said Salomé Sané, the nature and biodiversity campaigner for Greenpeace Canada.

The Building Canada Strong Act, or Bill C-39, is making its way through the House of Commons. The omnibus bill is proposing to amend several pieces of environmental legislation in order to fast-track pipelines, power lines, mines and other projects that fall under federal jurisdiction.

items: Critics accuse Carney government of proposing 'sacrifice zones' for the environment
Liberal MP calls for more safeguards in new bill to fast-track development projects

blocks.text: "We have the same federal government pushing for a very destructive bill under C-39 that will allow development projects to be built by bypassing, amongst other things, environmental regulations," Sané said.

"So our question to the government is, which is it? Are we protecting nature or are we destroying nature? Because going to COP to talk about nature protection and not defending nature at home will not allow us to deliver nature recovery."

items: Parks Canada plan to cut 500 jobs draws criticism from union

blocks.text: Debrusin responded to that criticism noting the government didn't move forward with some of the amendments it was contemplating due to pushback. She added the bill focuses on how projects get assessed, not weakening environmental standards.
"There's nothing in the policies we're putting forward that reduces our environmental standards," Dabrusin said.

Canada co-hosted with China the UN biodiversity conference in 2022. Countries signed the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which set a target of the world conserving 30 per cent of lands and waters by 2030.

items: Biodiversity agreement to protect planet reached at UN conference in Montreal

blocks.text: Since setting those targets, global progress has been slow according to UN Secretary General António Guterres.

"Even if current national commitments are met, only 26 per cent of terrestrial, and 12 per cent of marine ecosystems would be protected by 2030. That is well short of the promise made in Montreal," Guterres said in the Armenian capital last week.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

articles.title: The Marineland belugas keep dying. Was it a mistake to move them?
articles.summary: The deaths of six belugas at Marineland have raised questions about the impact of the transfers on their health and well-being and whether they were fit to travel. But was there ever a better option…

image.caption: Tofino, the last whale in captivity in Canada, is transported onto a truck via a sling before being moved to an aquarium in the U.S., in the final transfer of beluga whales out of the closed park, in Niagara Falls, Ont., on Aug. 31. Six of the transferred belugas have since died. (Carlos Osorio/The

blocks.text: A few months after a mass relocation effort that stretched across the Atlantic Ocean, six whales have died out of the 30 that were transferred from the now-shuttered Marineland theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont.

The most recent death, a beluga named Cyprus, was announced on Sunday by SeaWorld San Diego — one of five facilities in the U.S. and Spain that took in the marine mammals after Marineland said it could no longer care for them.

The deaths have raised questions about the impact of the transfers on their health and well-being and whether they were fit to travel, and rehashed concerns about the conditions they were living in during the years they spent at Marineland.
But was there ever a better option for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada?

Advocacy groups such as Animal Justice have pointed to the federal and provincial governments, as well as Marineland, saying they failed to properly plan for the animals' futures. Experts have said they're worried these deaths are just the beginning. Meanwhile, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans maintains the transfers were the best possible rescue plan.

Cyprus, a beluga whale who was rescued from Marineland in Niagara Falls in August, is shown in an undated photo published to social media by SeaWorld San Diego. SeaWorld announced the whale's death on Oct. 18. (SeaWorld San Diego/Facebook)

"This was, I would say, almost kind of a Hail Mary effort in terms of trying to make sure that we could provide a better life for these whales," Dr. Doug Whiteside, the head veterinarian at the Calgary Zoo and a member of the Canadian Veterinary Medical Association's animal welfare committee, told CBC News.

They were already under chronic stress from the conditions they faced at Marineland, Whiteside said. Transferring them caused additional stress, even though international regulations were followed and they went to high-calibre institutions to receive full-time care, he said.
"Is it a risk? Absolutely ... any sort of acute stress may push them over the edge," he said.

items: 'I tried to say goodbye and tried to tell him I love him': Canada's last captive whales leave Marineland

blocks.text: While we can't underestimate the stress of the transfers on the whales, that doesn't mean it's not in their best interests to try to give them a better life, said Angela Fernandez, director of the Animal Law Program at the University of Toronto's law faculty.
"People knew that there were stronger and weaker individuals in the mix, just like there would be among a group of 30 human retirees," Fernandez told CBC News.
"You would not evacuate an old-age home and take only the strong individuals if there is capacity to take everyone."
Why Marineland's last living belugas are on 'death watch'
What happened to Marineland?
Marineland, once Canada's most popular amusement park, has been the subject of controversy for years, with animal rights activists and others vehemently opposed to its practices.

A federal law passed in 2019 that bans keeping whales, dolphins and porpoises for breeding or entertainment in Canada shuttered its business model. Then it never recovered from the COVID-19 pandemic's tourism slump.

In 2024, the park was put up for sale and began relocating many of its animals. But in 2025, the federal government blocked Marineland's request to export the remaining belugas to an aquarium in China. Marineland responded by asking for emergency funding from Ottawa, warning that it might otherwise have no choice but to euthanize them.

items: Why it’s so hard to find a new home for Marineland’s 30 belugas

blocks.text: Releasing them into the wild would lead to certain death for the mammals raised in captivity, marine experts noted. And there was no appropriate seaside sanctuary for them in North America. A proposed sanctuary in Nova Scotia was still years away from being developed.

In May, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans endorsed a rescue plan to split up all remaining whales between Oceanogràfic València in Spain and four U.S. locations: Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and two SeaWorld facilities in San Diego and San Antonio, Texas.
By the end of August, the last whale had been shipped out.
PHOTOS | Belugas' journey out of Marineland:

This situation was entirely avoidable, said Camille Labchuk, executive director of Animal Justice, based in Toronto. The animal law advocacy group had pushed for a proactive plan to move the whales to a seaside sanctuary for years, she said, adding there was still time to plan a responsible transition after the 2019 legislation passed.
"It was obvious to everyone that Marineland would one day close, because the public no longer wants to see miserable whales swim in circles in tiny tanks," Labchuk said.
"A seaside sanctuary was always going to be a challenging undertaking ... but these challenges don't excuse the failure to plan for a better option."
Concerns about fitness to travel

Since their transfer, four whales have died at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, one whale and a dolphin have died at Oceanogràfic València and another whale has died at SeaWorld San Diego — representing one-fifth of the rescued whales.

The first, Peekachu, died on Aug. 25, about two weeks after arriving in Chicago. Rain was next on Sept. 2, followed by Osiris on Sept. 21, both of them also at Shedd. Necropsies for Peekachu and Rain, and preliminary results for Osiris, identified long-standing intestinal and liver issues that began before their rescue, the aquarium wrote in a blog post.

Jelly Bean died on Sept. 17 at Oceanogràfic València, and then Echo, a dolphin, died at the same facility on Sept. 23. They had been experiencing a list of health complications and organ abnormalities that may have developed prior to the transfer, the aquarium said in a news release.

items: Animal Justice urges investigation into Marineland beluga death in Chicago, wants relocation efforts halted
Marineland belugas that died in Chicago had chronic inflammatory disease, preliminary necropsy findings show

blocks.text: On Oct. 9, Shedd announced the death of Caspian two days earlier, noting it had been concerned about her health for weeks. The aquarium hasn't yet released her necropsy results. Cyprus, the sixth ill-fated beluga, died last weekend. SeaWorld San Diego said an ultrasound determined the animal's intestinal tract did not appear to be functioning normally.

There wasn't much transparency around the condition of the whales and dolphins before they were transferred due to their private ownership, U of T's Fernandez said. "After years and decades in captivity, it would be surprising if they didn’t all have significant health problems."
The deaths raise questions about whether the animals were fit to travel and whether every possible precaution was taken, Labchuk said, adding that the public deserves transparency.
'Heartbreaking,' says former trainer
Kristy Burgess, who worked as a trainer at Marineland from 2022 to 2025, called the deaths "heartbreaking."
Burgess has previously spoken out about the conditions at Marineland, noting that the beluga pools were in desperate need of repair and that the whales were eating paint peeling off the walls.

She now says she wishes there had been more opportunity for independent experts to contribute to the decision-making, as well as greater transparency around the planning, risks and ongoing health of the animals.
"Change has to come with a realistic, carefully considered plan for the animals themselves," Burgess said.
Former Marineland trainer Kristy Burgess says the beluga pools were in desperate need of repair and the whales were eating paint peeling off the walls. (Submitted by Kristy Burgess)
Whiteside, the Calgary Zoo's head veterinarian, said his understanding of the situation is that there simply wasn't a better option.
The belugas were in a "horrible situation" crowded into crumbling pools at Marineland, he said.
At least a transfer gave them a chance for a better life, he said, even if some didn't survive.

items: Former Marineland beluga whale dies at California theme park

blocks.text: The experience is a sad example of what can happen when institutions like Marineland aren't held to account, Whiteside said.
By not being held to account, Marineland allowed the animals to get to a state where they were chronically stressed, crowded in pools and eating paint, he said.
"Right from the get-go, this sets you up for potential failure."
'Their best chance of survival'
Before the animals' transport began, federal Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said she had taken reasonable steps to ensure their safety, including individual health assessments for each animal.
In a statement to CBC News on Wednesday, Thompson said she was still confident in the rescue plan, noting that the transfer was "a significant and complex undertaking."

"Marineland was no longer able to care for these animals. I remain confident that this rescue plan gives these belugas their best chance of survival and that they are being cared for by experienced professionals who are deeply committed to their welfare," she said.
The experts and advocates who spoke to CBC News say their concern now is for the fate of the remaining Marineland whales.
"It's almost a certainty that more belugas and dolphins will die," Labchuk of Animal Justice said.
But Fernandez said "that means 24 are safe, at least for now."
CBC News has reached out to Marineland for comment but has not received a response.
Beluga whales swim in a tank at Marineland in Niagara Falls on June 9, 2023. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

articles.title: In P.E.I., sweeping new strategy takes aim at ‘pervasive drinking culture’
articles.summary: From life-altering tragedies to everyday health risks, P.E.I. is taking direct aim at mitigating the toll of drinking. Advocates, are hoping a new provincial alcohol strategy will push Islanders to…

image.caption: After losing her son Jacob to a drunk driver in 2020, Brenda Simmons turned her grief into action, advising on PEI's new alcohol strategy. "Now we have something," she says, "let's all get behind this and have a different outcome for families." (Aaron Adetuyi/CBC)

blocks.text: LISTEN | Dr. Brian Goldman visits P.E.I. to learn about alcohol strategy:
White Coat Black Art26:30A bold plan to change PEI’s relationship with alcohol
Brenda Simmons is happy to see her son’s name at the top of a new monument in Charlottetown’s Joseph A. Ghiz Memorial Park. But she would still give anything for it not to be there.
The iron sculpture erected by the P.E.I. chapter of Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) is in the shape of the island, broken into three pieces.
“It’s to commemorate the way impaired driving breaks up communities, families and lives,” Simmons told Dr. Brian Goldman, host of White Coat, Black Art.

On June 12, 2020, 27-year-old Jacob Simmons was riding a bike on a country road near the family farm when he was struck and killed by an impaired driver who later admitted to having 13 drinks at home that day before getting behind the wheel.
Jacob Simmons was a keen marathon runner who had added biking to his training shortly before being struck and killed in the early evening hours of June 12, 2020. (Submitted by Brenda Simmons)

Six years later, in June of this year, P.E.I. released a sweeping alcohol strategy aimed at preventing tragic outcomes like Jacob’s – as well as the more everyday outcomes of heavy drinking, like cancer, heart disease, and cardiovascular disease. The province says the recommendations will come into effect in the months and years to come.
Though P.E.I.’s overall drinking rates are on par with Canadian averages, advocates for the strategy point to a culture on the island where heavy drinking is normalized.

items: As Canadians drink less, one rural P.E.I. community offers a different way to socialize

blocks.text: One statistic that hits close to home for Brenda Simmons is that P.E.I.’s impaired driving rates are nearly three times the national average. For her, the fact that the province is mostly rural, without public transit or Uber, is not enough to explain its prevalence.
“I would challenge you to find someone on this island who [cannot] say… yes, this happened to someone that I can name personally,” she said.
The strategy
Dr. Heather Morrison, P.E.I.’s chief public health officer, says alcohol is “very present” in the province.
“Alcohol is very mixed in with our social culture, our community culture.”

Her work on changing P.E.I.’s drinking culture goes way back, she says. After a good friend was killed by a drunk driver in middle school, Morrison got involved with the first chapter of Students Against Drunk Driving in Atlantic Canada.
“I can't remember not really thinking about the harms associated with alcohol,” she said.

P.E.I. Chief Public Health Officer Dr. Heather Morrison is targeting how much Islanders drink, rather than telling them not to. "I had someone recently say to me, 'I'm so glad you don't come out and say I cannot drink, but I'm really glad that you're telling me I should drink less because now I'll listen,'" she said. (Brian Goldman/CBC)

Morrison shepherded this alcohol strategy through five years of planning and consultation with more than 1,000 Islanders. She also worked with other government departments responsible for the pricing and sale of alcohol, public awareness, public safety and impaired-driving enforcement.

The strategy consists of 16 recommendations geared to approaching the problem from all angles, says Morrison. These include things like screening for high-risk drinking during medical appointments as well as targeted programs for things like reducing alcohol consumption among youth and monitoring those with fetal alcohol syndrome.

They also include a review of just how easy it is to buy alcohol, which could include reducing the number of stores or adjusting their operating hours. Currently 80 per cent of Islanders live within 10 minutes of a P.E.I. Liquor Control Commission outlet.
Morrison is hopeful the strategy’s focus on reducing consumption — rather than quitting altogether — will be key to its success.
What does P.E.I.’s new alcohol strategy mean for Islanders?

“We’ve tried to keep that emphasis around, there are harms associated with higher levels of drinking,” she said, pointing to a “Less Is Best” billboard encouraging Islanders that reducing their drinking by any amount is a step in the right direction.
Thousands of hospital visits
Dr. Trevor Jain says he sees the impacts of high-risk drinking every shift in the emergency department at Charlottetown’s Queen Elizabeth Hospital.
In fact, research shows it contributes to 7,000 emergency department visits and hospitalizations on P.E.I. annually.
“When you think of alcohol, you think of catastrophic motor vehicle collisions, and we see our fair share of those,” said Jain.

Dr. Trevor Jain is hoping that the new alcohol strategy's goals around "educating folks that alcohol is not a benign drink" will mean fewer patients coming to his ER at Queen Elizabeth Hospital suffering alcohol harms. (Brian Goldman/CBC)

But he says the heavy toll of alcohol presents itself in all kinds of other ways, too. When White Coat, Black Art paid a visit to the hospital earlier this month, Jain said he was about to go see a patient in alcohol withdrawal who needed help with symptoms.
What Jain calls the "culture of alcohol abuse" on P.E.I. has a more insidious side, too.
“It's like a spider web, right? It just doesn't affect the individual; it affects so many people around them. So although alcohol is a disease, it's a disease that's a contagion.”
Jain says he thinks the new alcohol strategy takes an excellent approach.

“Public health grabbing this by the horns… is going to help a lot of people,” he said. “It falls within that preventative medicine kind of matrix, and I think it will be extremely helpful to our local community.”
A model for other provinces
Adam Sherk, who co-authored Canada’s Guidance on Alcohol and Health, released in 2023, said other provinces should take note of the breadth of P.E.I.’s recommendations.

items: These Canadians passed on alcohol long before going 'dry' became trendy

blocks.text: Sherk, senior scientist for the Canadian Centre for Substance Use and Addiction (CCSA), also noted that P.E.I.’s strategy is more actionable than reports or plans from some other provinces, like B.C. or Saskatchewan, which he called “a little softer and not as directive.” Some provinces have not released any strategy on reducing alcohol harms.

As someone who researches alcohol-caused harms both in Canada and internationally, as well as the alcohol policies that might be able to mitigate those harms, Adam Sherk calls P.E.I.'s alcohol strategy "a very strong contribution to the alcohol policy landscape in Canada." (James Clay, CISUR)
Sherk says one of the best parts of P.E.I strategy is the recommendation to make boozier drinks more expensive, basing pricing on alcohol content, rather than the overall liquid volume of the drink.

Take two different canned beverages currently on P.E.I. liquor store shelves as an example. Lone Oak Vodka Seltzer and Black Fly Vodka Iced Tea are both 473 ml and cost $4.99. But the Black Fly has almost double the alcohol, seven per cent versus four per cent.

The alcohol strategy’s recommendation is to make the Black Fly more expensive, essentially eliminating “high bang for the buck products — very cheap alcohol that draws people into problems,” said Sherk.
Reducing the ‘alcohol deficit’
Morrison says the strategy also takes aim at the economic toll of P.E.I.’s drinking culture.

While alcohol sales on the Island pull in around $70 million per year in revenue, direct alcohol-related costs are estimated at over $131 million per year, according to data from the Canadian Alcohol Policy Evaluation.

items: Alcohol costs P.E.I. more than it brings in, new provincial strategy says

blocks.text: P.E.I.’s new strategy calls for a direct investment of three per cent of net alcohol profits back into community, education and harm-reduction efforts.
Brenda Simmons says she’s happy to see that. She works at roadside spot checks with the RCMP, where she and other members of MADD put a human face to the deadly consequences of drunk driving.
Simmons working at a roadside spot check in December 2024. (Connor Lamont/CBC)

She recalls one shift where all three officers accompanying them became tied up with impaired drivers — two identified through roadside screening and one who fled before reaching the checkpoint, requiring the third officer to give chase.
Simmons says she’s all too aware the tragedy she experienced might have been repeated had the officers not been there.
“It's beyond being a shame. Shame doesn't do it justice,” she said.
Dr. Morrison says it's the grief and passion of people like Simmons that keeps her motivated to see P.E.I.'s alcohol strategy implemented in specific and measurable ways.
“That's what helps us get across the finish line, and reminds us every day of why we need to keep doing this work.”

articles.title: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un travels to Chinese border city via newly opened bridge
articles.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un travelled to China’s border city of Dandong via a newly opened bridge linking the two countries, where he met a senior Chinese official.

image.caption: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrived in China via the newly opened bridge. Image: Florence Lo/REUTERS

blocks.text: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrived in China via the newly opened bridge on Saturday. He arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong via the New Yalu River Bridge linking the two countries.
China’s top political adviser Wang Huning met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, Chinese state media reported.
Wang conveyed President Xi Jinping’s "greetings and best wishes to Kim," Xinhua reported.
China and North Korea pledged to "strengthen strategic communication and cooperation to safeguard their sovereignty, security and development interests," Chinese state media said.
The two countries also vowed to expand people-to-people exchanges and economic and trade cooperation through the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge.
The four-lane bridge was completed in 2014 but remained unused for 12 years due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side.
It officially opened about a week ago, marking a step towards strengthening economic ties between the neighbouring countries.

China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a key source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the isolated, nuclear-armed state, although relations between the two have not always been smooth.
Kim’s trip coincides with key dates in China

The trip coincides with the anniversary of China’s entry into the Korean War, known in China as the "War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea." It remains unclear whether Kim will attend commemorative events.
During the 1950-53 war, Chinese troops fought alongside North Korea against South Korea and US-led United Nations forces.

Kim’s visit also comes ahead of a key political meeting in Beijing on Monday, when Chinese President Xi Jinping and other senior officials gather for the fifth plenary session of the Communist Party’s powerful Central Committee.

blocks.caption: Xi visited Pyongyang in June 2019, the first visit by a Chinese leader in 14 years (File image)Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bridge highlights North Korea's ties with China
The New Yalu River Bridge opened just over a month after North Korea and Russia inaugurated their first road bridge, which Pyongyang hailed as a sign of closer ties.
While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, trade with China could provide goods needed to develop its civilian economy, analysts say.

articles.title: Blaze engulfs Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain retreat in Bavaria
articles.summary:
About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle the blaze at former Nazi retreat in a remote part of southern Germany

German police said Saturday they had detained a suspect after a fire at Adolf…

blocks.text: German police said Saturday they had detained a suspect after a fire at Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat, known as the Eagle’s Nest, in the state of Bavaria.
About 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote and difficult-to-access Kehlsteinhaus residence, on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany.
Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said.
“A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody,” they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the blaze.
Police spokesperson Lisa Maier said firefighters struggled to tackle the fire due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000 feet).
The building was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.
Authorities were alerted to the fire on Friday evening, when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.50pm (1950 GMT), police said.
No potential reason for the fire was given, but the German media reported that the investigators suspected it was the result of arson.
As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle’s Nest was still engulfed in flames in the early hours of Saturday, a weather camera showed.
Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an AFP photographer.
The firefighters found no one inside the building.
Maier said police were still investigating but will hold a news conference later on Saturday.
German tabloid Bild reported that the authorities had arrested a motorcyclist they came across on their way to the scene.

Built between 1937 and 1938, the Eagle’s Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and Communists in the Holocaust.
It was designed to serve as a monument to Hitler’s rule, although the dictator rarely visited the complex.
It survived the second world war undamaged, and since 1952 has hosted an exhibition recounting the house’s Nazi history and a restaurant.

articles.title: Minneapolis withdrawal was 'surrender', Trump's ex-border patrol chief tells BBC
articles.summary: Greg Bovino was the public face of the controversial immigration enforcement operation in the city earlier this year.

blocks.text: The former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the highly controversial deportation drive in Minneapolis earlier this year has defended the operation, describing the withdrawal of agents from the city as a "surrender" by the Trump administration.

In an interview with the BBC, Greg Bovino also said he was "not responding" to a lawsuit filed by the family of a woman shot dead during the operation. He appeared to dismiss the legal action, praising the officers deployed to Minneapolis and saying "people do lawsuits all the time".
Bovino, 56, was removed from his role shortly after the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.

The two shootings, which were captured on video, triggered a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. Trump then said he was "going to de-escalate a little bit" and withdrew hundreds of immigration agents from the city.

Earlier this month, Good's family filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration over her killing, alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of protesters.

One of the lawsuits names several top officials, including Bovino and Jonathan Ross, the agent who shot Good, "for their respective individual roles in the operation that led to Renee's death". It alleges that the government's operation in Minneapolis created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence".

Asked about Bovino's remarks, the family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and could not be "judge, jury, and executioner". They added: "Our legal team looks forward to the depositions of Mr Bovino and all of the defendants in this matter".
A White House spokeswoman previously called the lawsuits "baseless".

Speaking in Detroit where he was campaigning for tougher immigration enforcement, Bovino said the administration "threw the towel in" and called for more deportations, which he said were now at a "virtual standstill".
He added that he regretted "not going harder in Minnesota and arresting even more illegal aliens".
Bovino said his agents in Minneapolis were the "real victims" of what he called "the most violence that any law enforcement mission ever in the history of the United States has been up against".

Challenged by the BBC over how immigration agents handled both shooting incidents, Bovino rejected suggestions that video evidence undermined his claim that Good and Pretti had intended to harm the agents.
"The evidence is that violence was perpetrated against agents of the US government, and this is a society of laws and people need to follow the law. If not, there are consequences," he said.

Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake".
The withdrawal from Minnesota, which saw some 700 immigration agents leave the state, also saw Bovino removed from his post. The operation was taken over by the White House 'border tsar' Tom Homan.
When asked why he was removed, Bovino told the BBC: "You'd have to ask the administration. I still haven't gotten the final word on that."

articles.title: Why Russia's arrest of Japanese journalist is the latest sign of deteriorating ties between the countries.
articles.summary: Japan is demanding access to a journalist who was arrested by Russian security services. The Kremlin claims that Japan is using journalists as spies.

image.caption: Journalist Yuki Imai seen being taken into custody by Russian security agents Image: Russian Federal Security Service/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Japanese Foreign Ministry officials were in Moscow this week in an attempt to contact a journalist arrested in Russia's far east on allegations of spying.

Journalist Yuki Imai was arrested on October 14 by Russia's FSB security service in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin Island. Televised footage of the arrest showed FSB officers barging into his hotel room as he slept.

The correspondent for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was accused of attempting to obtain information on soldiers in the region, which is near the Kiril islands, a geopolitical sore spot in Russia-Japan relations.

Russian authorities quickly transferred him to Lefortovo Prison in Moscow, where a court ordered him to be held in pretrial detention until at least December 12. If convicted, 34-year-old Imai faces up to 20 years in jail, according to the International Federation of Journalists, which has called for his immediate release.
Officials from the Japanese embassy in Moscow have been denied access to Imai. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned the arrest and dismissed the claim that Imai was a spy.

Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev said Imai had been caught "red-handed," the official TASS news agency reported. Nozdrev has claimed that Japanese intelligence agencies use journalists to collect classified information with the goal of "undermining Russia's security and defense capability."
Russia accuses journalists of being 'spies'

Yoji Gomi, a veteran journalist and author who has reported from across Asia, told DW that Japanese journalists may occasionally meet with diplomats in the course of their work and "share thoughts and impressions." However, he rejects the idea that reporters are paid spies.
"One-party nations often see foreign correspondents as spies because that is exactly what they use their journalists for," he said.

"I can completely see how the Russians decided that Imai was a spy, as it is how they operate, plus he was in a sensitive part of Russia where there are lots of North Korean laborers that they want to keep quiet," Gomi added.
Japan condemns Putin visit to disputed Kuril Islands

Stephen Nagy, a professor of international relations at Tokyo's International Christian University, told DW that Russia might see Imai as a bargaining chip it can use to exchange for nationals detained overseas.
Nagy doubts that Japan will give in to pressure.

"They are going to resist because it means that Russia, or any other country, can then just seize a Japanese national, put them on trial for espionage and demand the release of one of their people," he said.
"It would set a dangerous precedent," he added.
The arrest comes after a member of the Russia-linked hacking group Qilin was arrested in Japan and extradited to Germany to face charges in connection with a 2024 cyberattack on a logistics center.

The last time a journalist was arrested in Russia was in 2019 for "attempting to obtain classified information about Russia's military potential in the Far East," Russia's Interfax news agency reported. However, in this case, the journalist was quickly released.

Imai's case is perhaps the most serious since 2023, when Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich was arrested in Russia and sentenced to 16 years in a penal colony before being released in a prisoner exchange with Western countries in 2024.

blocks.caption: Russia has previously arrested foreign journalists for prisoner exchanges. US reporter Evan Gershkovich is seen here in a Moscow court.Image: Dmitry Serebryakov/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Strained Japan-Russia ties
Imai's arrest is the latest in a series of incidents that have sent bilateral relations into a tailspin.

Nagy said Imai's seizure was designed to put pressure on Tokyo. He added this is part of a coordinated approach with China to isolate Japan at a time when the US is preoccupied with domestic issues and the conflict in the Middle East.

"Moscow and Beijing are coordinating to create the image that Japan is not a reformed member of the international community but still the military state of the 1930s and that it poses a threat to stability in the Indo-Pacific region," Nagy said.

"This is all designed to smear Japan's efforts to lead diplomacy in the region at a time when the US is perhaps distracted," he said. "And it does not even matter much that it is not true; they will just continue to repeat the claim to discredit and weaken Tokyo."
Decadeslong row over disputed islands

Tadashi Anno, a professor of politics at Tokyo's Sophia University, told DW that he believes Japan had been working hard to maintain a stable relationship with Russia, even after Tokyo joined international condemnation of the invasion of Ukraine.
Anno said Russia's timing in turning up the heat on Japan was puzzling.
"Japan condemned the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 because it was a fundamental violation of international law, but Russia is only now pushing back hard," he said.
At the center of deteriorating ties is a territorial dispute about a chain of islands off the far north of Japan that were seized by Soviet forces after Japan's surrender in World War II.

There had been hopes in the past in Tokyo that a concerted diplomatic effort could be sufficient to convince Russia to return the islands — known as the Northern Territories in Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia — to Japanese sovereignty.
That campaign has faltered in the past couple of years, and was further dented when Japan announced in the spring that it would be joining the NATO initiative to provide nonlethal assistance to Kyiv.

In August, President Vladimir Putin visited the disputed islands, becoming only the second Russian leader to do so. Earlier this month, a delegation of Chinese businesspeople was welcomed on one of the islands, and talks are underway on the possibility of economic cooperation.

articles.title: Taiwan: Typhoon Champi leaves 1 dead, over 500 injured
articles.summary: After killing one person and causing major disruptions in Taiwan, Typhoon Champi is now headed towards China.

image.caption: More than 500 people were injured as Typhoon Champi swept through TaiwanImage: cnsphoto/REUTERS

blocks.text: Typhoon Champi killed at least one person and left more than 500 people with injuries as it passed through Taiwan on Saturday.
Taiwan's fire department said the death toll remained at 1 a man swept ​away by waves from the island of Liuqiu, with 527 injuries during the heavy wind and torrential rain.
Several parts in Taiwan received heavy rain and strong winds that prompted authorities to cut off power, leaving thousands of people without power supply.
Some 280,000 households were knocked out of power, according to United Daily News, a local Taiwanese newspaper. By Saturday morning, the power supply was restored to 80% of the households.

blocks.caption: Despite weakening, Champi is still packing strong winds near its centerImage: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

blocks.text: Champi also led to 259 flights cancellations, an improvement from Friday, ⁠when ​the number was almost 1,000, the Transport Ministry said.
Several trees were downed amid strong gusts In the capital Taipei.
Authorities in several districts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second day of office and school closures on Saturday.
Champi headed to China
The typhoon continued to weaken as it moved north towards the Chinese coast though it was not expected to make landfall there.
Chinese authorities have sent a team to ​the eastern province of Zhejiang as Champi ⁠approached, warning of strong winds and heavy rain through Sunday.

blocks.caption: Schools and offices were closed in several districts in Taiwan because of ChampiImage: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

blocks.text: It said it had readied 400 rescue workers and 600 pieces of equipment, ⁠while more than 41,000 firefighters were on ​emergency duty.

Typhoon Champi started out as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year. While it is weakening, Champi is still packing ​gusts of around 78 km/h (126 mph) near its center, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA).

articles.title: How Brazil's changing working class is reshaping the presidential race
articles.summary: Calls for change present a challenge to President Lula in the second round of the election on Sunday.

blocks.text: A student at a rally for President Lula da Silva
ByIone Wells
Reporting fromSão Paulo and Rio de Janeiro
In the sprawling former industrial city of Osasco, shuttered factories have given way to a shopping malls and delivery app tech companies in what is now dubbed São Paulo's "Silicon Valley."

The municipality voted for Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in 2022 but switched to the right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of Brazil's presidential election this month. Bolsonaro won that vote - and now the two men face a run-off on Sunday. Since 1989, every first-round winner has gone on to be elected president.
Like many of President Lula's traditional supporters, Gilberto Almazan, who leads a metalworkers' union here, is visibly worried.

He cries when he tells Lula's life story: a boy who grew up in hunger in the north-east, who became a metalworker, then a union leader, then a three-time president. But he's candid about how things have changed here and how the union movement that was so integral to Lula's support base is stuck in the "Middle Ages", and struggling to keep up.
"We had strong deindustrialisation here," Almazan says. "The profile of the working class changed. They are no longer predominantly industrial workers, they are service workers.
"Metal, chemical, textile factories disappeared. And five malls were built."

The word "change" comes up repeatedly among Bolsonaro supporters here. Many struggle to name specific Bolsonaro policies they like but know they want to try something different: frustrated by the economy, crime and corruption in politics – even though Flávio has been faced accusations of corruption too, which he denies.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tairine says high prices are a problem for her

blocks.text: Tairine says high prices are a problem for her
"He brings the hope of change, that we can have a different Brazil," says lawyer Gisele Bonfim in Osasco, who decided to vote for Bolsonaro after supporting Lula in 2022.

Lula's re-election campaign has been hampered by voters turning away from him. In some cases, their frustration drove abstention, which was higher than average this year, but others like Gisele actively wanted something new.
One major reason for that is Brazil's working class has transformed seismically in places like Osasco.
Near one large shopping mall lies an open-air market where this shift is noticeable. Everyone is touting products, armed with a portable card machine.

Tairine, who sells hot dogs, used to abstain from voting, even though - as voting is compulsory in Brazil - not going to the polls incurs a fine. This year, she plans to vote for Bolsonaro. She points to high taxes paid on "everything" she buys and says these make it "so difficult for a poor person" dealing with inflation, arguing "nothing has changed" since Lula became president again.
Flávio Bolsonaro has proposed cutting government spending, government ministries, and some taxes - though he has said he'd maintain some of Lula's flagship welfare programmes.
A new working class

For his supporters, Lula is a working-class hero credited with advancing workers' rights through organising strikes and lifting millions of people out of poverty with generous social welfare programmes as president.

But across Brazil millions now work in the gig economy, a phenomenon Almazan calls "Uber-isation": driving for Uber, delivering food, or running small businesses from market stalls to providing at-home beauty treatments.
"There are a lot of workers who need more freedom, flexibility of days and hours," he says, rather than the welfare and collective action Lula offered.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Robson used to support Lula but has since switched to support Bolsonaro

blocks.text: Robson used to support Lula but has since switched to support Bolsonaro

Richard Lapper, who has written biographies of both Lula and Jair Bolsonaro – Flavio's father who was president from 2019-2022 - says the rise of individualised work and the decline of manufacturing caused by globalisation are not unique to Brazil. But because Brazil industrialised late and deindustrialised early, he argues, the effects have been sharper here. He calls Lula a "victim of his own success."

Unemployment fell to a record low, and Brazil was taken off the United Nation's Hunger Map during Lula's current presidency. But Lapper describes a crisis of "expectations" where people are now better off but don't feel it because prices have risen and household debt and interest rates are high.
Robson, 53, is a municipal civil servant in Osasco. Originally from Lula's north-eastern home state of Pernambuco, he grew up supporting him.

But he describes a country now running deficits and says its citizens are enduring the "worst phase" of its tax burden, which he blames on the Lula government's "mismanagement" of the economy and high public spending.
"Now you have to make choices: pay an instalment for your car, or put food on the table," he says.
Lula's comeback strategy

In some areas, Lula lost votes compared to 2022, even though Bolsonaro did not gain more than his father did then: 33 million people did not vote in the first round, the highest abstention since 1998.

In response, Lula's campaign has focused on mobilising hundreds of thousands of people – particularly students – on to the streets to get the vote out for round two. It claims one rally in São Paulo attracted about a million people.
"A lot of people didn't vote, they thought it wouldn't change anything," says one supporter, Leila. "Our fight is to make those people believe their vote changes things."
Aerial videos of these huge demonstrations have been plastered across social media. An image of a topless man with a six-pack waving a Lula flag at one has been shared tens of millions of times.
The strategy is that their revolution will not be televised, but it should ideally go viral.

Lula, 80, has also been using social media to dismiss criticisms that he is past his prime: calling himself the "king of selfies" and posting videos showing him running from A to B on the campaign trail.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Some people who live in the favelas fear security forces entering if Bolsonaro is elected

blocks.text: Some people who live in the favelas fear security forces entering if Bolsonaro is elected
In Maré, one of Rio's largest favelas which is controlled by rival gangs, abstention was higher than average.

This dented Lula's support, even though he still won here: among Brazil's very poorest, Lula's welfare initiatives clearly do still resonate. One 18-year-old mother in Maré, Vitoria, earns less than £300 a month and praises Lula's government for increasing the minimum wage, giving workers the right to two days off, and providing essential medicines for free.
She is sceptical of Bolsonaro's plans to designate the gang which controls this part of the favela, Comando Vermelho, as a terrorist organisation, which he lobbied the US to do earlier this year.

She thinks it will lead to authorities entering the favela to "kill, destroy, ruin families, leave blood and bodies on the ground", citing a police raid in Rio last year that killed more than 130 people.
Another resident, Andreza Dionísio, blames high abstention rates here on both last-minute changes to polling station locations, but also "a sense of hopelessness about the future."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Many Brazilians now worship in evangelical churches like the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo

blocks.text: Many Brazilians now worship in evangelical churches like the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo

Increasingly, that void of hope is being filled by the growth of the evangelical church: about a quarter of Brazilians are now evangelical. Its mega-churches offer not just a spiritual home but support with issues like childcare, employment advice and even food.
Its conservative pastors are some of Brazil's most powerful political operators.

Silas Malafaia, who has millions of followers on social media, leads the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo headquartered in the lower middle-class neighbourhood of Penha in Rio de Janeiro. He is being investigated for allegedly obstructing the coup trial of Jair Bolsonaro, which he denies and calls politically motivated.

At one two-hour sermon he preaches messages of self-improvement to an emotional crowd of hundreds, interrupted occasionally for live music interludes and breaks to collect money with card machines. The whole event is live-streamed on YouTube.

Afterwards, in his office adorned with a photo of him and the former president Jair Bolsonaro, at whose wedding he officiated, he told the BBC that without the evangelical church in working-class neighbourhoods the country would be "in a state worse than you can imagine".
"It gives these people meaning. To better their lives."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pastor Silas Malafaia officiated at Jair Bolsonaro's wedding

blocks.text: Pastor Silas Malafaia officiated at Jair Bolsonaro's wedding
He argues Flávio Bolsonaro shares the church's values: for family, and against gender "ideology" and abortion.

The church is driving some to actively vote for Flávio Bolsonaro, but among much of Brazil's new working class, the first round feels more like a rejection of President Lula than an endorsement of his rival.
"There will never be another Lula," Gilberto Almazan fears. He intends this as a compliment, but Brazil's changing world of work means it's also probably true.
While Lula's past story still stirs great emotion for people like Almazan, his political fate may depend on whether voters think he can now offer Brazil a new one.

articles.title: India news: Andhra, Odisha brace for severe storm
articles.summary: The weather department warned that a depression over the Bay of Bengal could escalate into a very severe cyclonic storm before crossing the Andhra Pradesh coast, with winds reaching 140 km/h. DW has…

image.caption: In 2023, India's deadliest cyclone season left 523 people dead and caused an estimated $2.5 billion (€2.15 billion) in damages [FILE: December 8, 2022, ]Image: ARUN SANKAR/AFP

blocks.text: Parts of the states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha were on alert on Sunday as India's weather department warned of an incoming severe cyclonic storm over Bay of Bengal.

According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Sunday, a depression over the east-central Bay of Bengal is likely to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm by Tuesday and cross the Andhra Pradesh coast between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam.
IMD said the "maximum sustained wind speed of 115-125 km/h gusting to 140 km/h by forenoon" is expected by October 28, when the storm is likely to make landfall.

Schools and colleges in five southern Odisha districts bordering Andhra Pradesh will stay closed on October 28 and 29, the Indian Express newspaper reported,as authorities took stock of the situation.
President Droupadi Murmu's scheduled two-day visit to Odisha on October 28-29 has also been postponed to early November due to the impending cyclone, according to the paper.

articles.title: Arrest made after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.summary: Around 200 emergency personnel are deployed to fight the blaze at the Nazi dictator's Alpine residence in Germany.

blocks.text: Police in the south German state of Bavaria have detained a suspect during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 (19:15 GMT) on Friday, and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Difficult terrain was hindering efforts to extinguish the blaze and it was still burning early on Saturday, police said, with some 200 emergency personnel deployed. There were no reports of injuries.
The Nazi dictator used the retreat, which lies above the town of Berchtesgaden, as a part-time seat of government and met commanders there to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941.
A criminal investigation is under way to determine whether the suspect is connected to the fire.
Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.

articles.title: Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat catches fire, police say
articles.summary: Authorities have arrested a suspect as firemen try to put out the fire in Bavaria, near the Austrian border.

image.caption: The site once housed the Nazi leader's heavily fortified country residence [FILE: Jun 21, 2004]Image: Peter Kneffel/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A fire broke out at the Kehlsteinhaus retreat, more commonly known as Adolf Hitler's Eagle's Nest, on Friday evening, Bavarian police said.
The Kehlsteinhaus was engulfed in flames, a police statement read, adding that a suspect has been arrested and the incident was being criminally investigated.
What do we know so far about the Kehlsteinhaus fire?
A fire alarm went off at the Kehlsteinhaus on the Obersalzberg in Berchtesgaden at around 9:15 p.m. local time (1915 GMT) on Friday, the police said in a statement.
"The fire brigades, who were alerted immediately, could already see flames clearly visible at the Kehlsteinhaus as they approached," the police statement read.
Firefighters struggled to reach the Kehlsteinhaus, which sits at some 1,834 meters (6,017 feet) above sea level, with their engines.
Police added that the building and its immediate vicinity could only be entered while wearing respiratory protective equipment (RPE).
Police said they were unaware of any injuries as of yet.
The site once housed Hitler's heavily fortified country residence, where he is believed to have partially written his book "Mein Kampf."
It remains a symbol of the Nazi regime and is among only a few monuments of the Hitler era that survived the World War II bombing unscathed. Today, it is home to a popular restaurant.

articles.title: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
articles.summary:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled

Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more…

blocks.text: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.

Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan.

blocks.caption: Waves generated by Typhoon Champi crash against a seawall in Keelung. Photograph: Ann Wang/Reuters

blocks.text: Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on…

blocks.text: Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.
The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 180km (110 miles) south of the capital, Amman.

Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church.
Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church.

Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. “It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire,” Halasa said.

He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan’s security services did not immediately release details.

A government statement said that the attack was “carried out by unknown assailants,” but didn’t say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that “investigations are under way at full speed”.
Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom’s Petra news agency.
Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff.
Jordan’s health minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition.

King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan “will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties” and offered his “deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded”.

Jordan’s prime minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism.
Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman.

Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world’s foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday’s shooting, calling it a “heinous terrorist attack.”
Iraqi foreign minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and “affirmed Iraq’s solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism”, Hussein’s office said in a statement.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as “especially heinous,” spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said. “The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account.”

articles.title: Australian MP's condition improves after alleged car attack
articles.summary: The Independent MP is now in a serious but stable condition, according to the Melbourne hospital.

blocks.text: Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.
Police said more charges might be laid, including attempted murder.
His lawyer said his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Investigators are looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident.
Nugent's family has said they were long-time friends with Haines.

Shortly after the alleged attack, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told ABC television that there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia.
Haines, known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action, entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife.

articles.title: Embattled Greens senator Jordon Steele-John confirms leave from parliament after allegations against him made public
articles.summary:
WA politician says he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be ‘unacceptable’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament next week as the embattled Greens senator releases a letter detailing the allegations against him.
After days of confusion following historical complaints about alleged misconduct were publicly aired in the media, Steele-John posted a statement to social media late Friday night.

In the statement, the Western Australian senator said he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be “unacceptable”. He will instead focus on seeing through an independent investigation to its conclusion, he said.

“Over the past few days there has been a growing chorus calling on me not to attend parliament next week. I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable,” Steele-John said.
Steele-John said a precedent of keeping parliamentarians out of parliament after “allegations of allegations” are made had now been set.
“Had an allegation or complaint been made against me, I would have taken these actions immediately,” he said.

The 32-year-old senator’s attendance in parliament for the remainder of the year had been uncertain after a public stoush with the party’s leader, David Shoebridge, over whether he was on leave while an investigation was undertaken into allegations he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.
The complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens and have been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.
Shoebridge claimed Steele-John had requested leave and he accepted it last week after seven party members penned a letter to the leader urging an investigation into the claims.

The three-page letter sent on 13 October, and first published by the Nine newspapers, said the authors had been “made aware of multiple allegations of serious misconduct” against Steele-John about his “behaviour in the presence of women”.
The letter referred to an allegation of sexual harassment at a Greens campaign event in 2024 that the alleged victim had not reported out of fear and backlash. The letter provided no further detail.
In another, the authors referred to an allegation of “serious sexual misconduct” in 2025.
Also contained in the letter was a reference to a disparaging nickname for Steele-John – “feels on wheels” – which the authors said implied he had a reputation for acting inappropriately.

“To be clear, all signatories to this letter know that an allegation does not equate to a fact and/or guilt. We simply believe that it is in the party’s best interests to ensure that every allegation is investigated thoroughly, in alignment with community and member expectations,” the letter’s authors wrote.

Steele-John was defiant in a lengthy statement last Sunday, rejecting the allegations against him, denying he agreed to take leave from parliament and accusing an internal faction within the Greens of playing “nasty political games” in their decision to release the letter to the media.

Steele-John said any claims of his alleged behaviour should be investigated “fairly and thoroughly” but accused an “unofficial faction” within the WA branch had released the complaint letter to the media in a bid to oust him from the Senate.
Guardian Australia has confirmed the WA police told Steele-John the investigation was closed in May with no charges.

articles.title: Helen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attack
articles.summary:
Independent MP now serious but stable, according to update from Melbourne’s Alfred hospital

  • Get our breaking news…

blocks.text: Independent MP Helen Haines’s condition has been downgraded to serious but stable after she lost both legs following an alleged attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria on Monday afternoon.
The Alfred hospital in Melbourne provided an update on Haines’s condition on Saturday morning.
“The patient is in a serious but stable condition at The Alfred on Saturday morning,” a spokesperson for the hospital said.

Haines, the federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg on Tuesday, but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.

Police on Tuesday charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Police have since charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.
Nugent appeared in court on Wednesday and did not apply for bail.
On Friday, an update on Haines’s social media accounts said her staff were working to reopen her electorate offices next Thursday.
“What happened on Monday has deeply affected Helen’s family and all of her staff. Many of us witnessed the incident and some were among the first to come to her aid,” the post read.

“As Helen takes the time she needs to recover, we will take time to look after ourselves and one another, too. Healing will take time, and we ask for your understanding as we navigate the days and weeks ahead.”
The alleged attack on Haines has reverberated through Australian politics, prompting conversations about the temperature of political debate and mental services in regional Victoria.

articles.title: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom
articles.summary: From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on some products, including certain machinery, and placed on others, such as carpets.

blocks.text: The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key US Senate race said she had lobbied for the change.
From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment", the White House said on Friday.
Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.
The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (£15bn) worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August.
Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures in response to the US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers".
Last month, Carney matched the US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US car, dairy and alcohol exports.
The White House said that, while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products".
It said the action reflected US President Donald Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade".
